utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I finished yesterday talking about KVM's report, Kosovo "As Seen, As Told", which concluded that one of the main threats to the Serb community was the UCK, the KLA. Similarly, ECMM and KDOM mobile teams operating during the indictment period on the ground documented instances of KLA abductions, including victims in our case both Albanians and Serbs. For example, ECMM reported on the kidnapping of Shaban Hoti in their report of 26 to -- the 20th to the 26th of July, 1998. And that's included in the annexes to P230. I previously referred to the 29th of June ECMM report which documented the kidnappings of Ivan and Vojko Bakrac, Stamen Genov and Djordje Cuk. Let me here correct a mistake in the Defence brief. This is at paragraph 167 where it states that Djordje Cuk was a serving member of the VJ. That's not true. Stamen Genov is the only victim in this case who was a member of the VJ. The only cite in support for that clearly false statement in the Defence briefs is transcript page 317. Your Honours, if you take a look at pages 316 to 317, I think you'll see that there's no support there for the proposition that Cuk was a VJ member. At the time he was kidnapped, Djordje Cuk was a Serb refugee. That's shown by P181, the 92 bis statement of his surviving brother, another refugee. And Vojko Bakrac testified that Djordje Cuk, to his knowledge, was a refugee and was not a member of any armed group or police or military. That's at page 1296. Fatmir Limaj here in his testimony admitted to KLA crimes committed against civilians. One of the most notorious instances of KLA attacks on civilians is the kidnapping and killing of civilians in Rahovec. Approximately 85 civilians were kidnapped in July 1998. That's documented in the Human Rights Watch report in evidence at P212, tab 5. Susan Ringaard Pedersen's testimony corroborates those findings from Human Rights Watch. She testified that women from Rahovec came and reported that their husbands, their sons had been taken by the KLA and had never been returned. Mr. Limaj accepted before you that Rahovec was a black stain on the KLA, not just because of the losses suffered by KLA soldiers but because of the killings and kidnappings of Serb civilians. I'll talk just for a moment now about crimes against Albanian civilians. Mr. Whiting's talked about this as well as Mr. Black, so I won't spend much time. Beginning in 1997, the General Staff of the KLA repeatedly stated in official communiques that it was targeting so-called collaborators for death. I won't go through those communiques. They're referenced in paragraph 166 of our brief in the footnotes to that paragraph. Mr. Whiting has described to you and the evidence has shown that the barest allegation and the complete lack of any form of hearing or due process led to the murders of Albanian civilians. Jakup Krasniqi, the spokesman for the KLA, admitted that they had executed collaborators exactly as claimed in the communiques which he authenticated. Krasniqi stated that these men were not tried in courts but that "they were executed or killed" by the KLA in the field at the discretion of local commanders. And again, specific murders referenced in those communiques he confirmed had in fact taken place. In their brief beginning at paragraph 375, the Defence concede that there is no requirement or element of the existence of a plan or policy for crimes against humanity. However, as far as the existence of a policy is evidence of systematic attack, plainly here there was such a policy. As Mr. Whiting said yesterday, Limaj himself has testified that the KLA had a policy of targeting people suspected of collaboration. In addition to Mr. Krasniqi and Mr. Limaj's admissions, there is the evidence of KLA crimes committed against Albanian civilians which are strikingly similar to the crimes committed in the Lapusnik prison. I point you to the testimony of Witness L95. He spoke about the detention and murder of collaborators on the flimsiest of pretexts took place during our indictment period at a different location. That's at 4247 to 4258 of the record. I'm just about done, Your Honours, and I conclude by remembering the view of the ICRC, that the protections of Common Article 3 should be applied as widely as possible to protect the victims of armed conflicts. The Defence has argued here and will argue that there was no armed conflict. Therefore, the jurisdictional element of the Tribunal has not been met and the perpetrators on both sides, therefore, should be able to escape with impunity from the crimes they've committed. This is a sort of recurrent theme for the Defence. No camp, no General Staff, no armed conflict even in the face of overwhelming evidence to the contrary. Violent armed confrontations proven in this trial weren't terrorist acts or weren't acts of banditry. This wasn't a short-lived or unorganised insurrection. We've seen an intense, prolonged armed conflict in which civilians on both sides paid a heavy price. I'm sure you'll find that those victims are due the protections of international law. I'll give the floor back to Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please Your Honours, I will now briefly address the Chamber on the issue of sentencing. A strong argument could be made that all accused convicted of the types of crimes charged against these three accused should receive a sentence of life in prison. Certainly in most jurisdictions, most domestic jurisdictions around the world, this would be the case. However, that is not the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, which has established an internal scale as well as internal guidelines to evaluate sentences in war crime cases. Article 24 of the Statute and Rule 101 of the Rules govern sentencing. The first factor to consider requires the Chamber to take into account the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia, though the law is clear that the Chamber is not bound by this practice and can impose a higher sentence. This particular factor was considered by this Chamber in the Strugar judgement, and I shall not dwell on it. In the submission of the Prosecution, under Articles 142, 148, and 38 of the SFRY Code, the sentencing range for the crimes charged in this case would be between five and 20 years in the former Yugoslavia. The gravity of the offence is the next factor to consider, and the Appeals Chamber has held that it is the primary consideration in imposing sentence. In this case, the accused bear the responsibility for the operation, over a nearly two-month period, of an extremely brutal and vicious prison camp where prisoners were subjected to inhumane conditions, mistreatment, beatings, torture, and murder. The only reason the prison was shut down, we submit, was that the Serbian forces overran Lapusnik at the end of July 1998. The evidence has proven that at least 23 men were murdered in connection with the prison camp in Lapusnik. In evaluating the seriousness of this case, it would be a mistake, in the Prosecution's submission, simply to compare the crime base of this case with the crime bases of other cases. The crime base in this case must be evaluated in context, in the context of the war that was then going on in Kosovo and in the context of the strength and development of the KLA. In addition, there are a number of aggravating circumstances to consider. The Appeals Chamber listed some potential aggravating circumstances in the Blaskic appeal judgement at paragraph 686 and a number imply in this case: discriminatory intent, which can be an aggravating factor when discriminatory intent is not an element of the crime; length of time during which the crime continued; active and direct criminal participation; premeditation; the violent and humiliating nature of the acts and the vulnerability of the victims; the status of the victims, including youthful age, number, and the effect of the crimes on them; civilian detainees; character of the accused, which includes remorse or lack of remorse; and circumstances of the offences generally. First, with respect to discriminatory intent. The crimes committed against the Serb victims were plainly committed with discriminatory intent. The Serbs were singled out for mistreatment and murder simply because they were Serb. It can also be argued that the crimes committed against the Albanian victims were also committed with discriminatory intent because the Albanians were targeted solely because of their association with Serbs. Second, the crimes in this case, we submit, were ongoing, premeditated, and organised, and they were extraordinarily violent and humiliating. Third, the Prosecution submits that many of the victims in this case were in fact vulnerable. Some of the victims were vulnerable because of personal circumstances such as age or infirmity. In addition, the Prosecution submits that the Albanian victims in this case were also particularly vulnerable. Ordinarily in a conflict victims of war crimes have at the very least a state or a military force that will, if possible, fight on their behalf or attempt to obtain their release if they are being detained unlawfully. In this case, however, the Albanian victims had nobody. They were victimised by their own army, and were therefore particularly vulnerable. Fourth, another aggravating factor is the fact that all three accused have lied about the existence of the camp in Lapusnik and their roles in the camp. The cover-up of the camp began was the camp was still operating. The evidence shows that the victims who were released were required to swear not to reveal what had happened in Lapusnik. During the investigation of this case, Isak Musliu was interviewed and denied the existence of a camp in Lapusnik. This factor is particularly aggravating, however, for Fatmir Limaj, who testified during trial and denied the existence of the camp in Lapusnik and his role in it. And for Haradin Bala, who made a statement during trial denying that in his belief anybody in the KLA could ever commit the crimes charged here, and of course denying his own role in the crimes. Neither one was required to say something in this trial, to say anything in this trial, and both could have remained silent. They chose, however, to speak, and in our submission sought to mislead the Court with their words. In the final brief, as Mr. Black has already pointed out, the Defence does not just deny the existence of the camp at Lapusnik but the existence of any such camp, stating in paragraph 178 that "It is plain that the KLA would have lacked the ability to run any prison camp." Another aggravating factor with respect to Fatmir Limaj in particular and also to Isak Musliu is their positions of authority which were abused by their participation in the operation of the prison at Lapusnik. Finally, the Chamber should consider the effect on the victims and the relatives of the victims. This Chamber has heard from survivors of the camp as well as from family members of victims who were killed. It is clear that the survivors of the camp are to this day traumatised and continue to suffer both physical and psychological pain, and are in many cases destroyed by what happened to them. There are families all over Kosovo and elsewhere who suffer every day because of what happened at Lapusnik. Are there mitigating factors? Fatmir Limaj suggests that he expressed remorse for the victims in his opening statement of the trial, pointing in paragraph 415 of their brief to just two sentences of that lengthy opening. The Prosecution submits that these tepid sentences fail to express any genuine remorse for the victims, and in fact are more focused on shifting blame to others. In Limaj's testimony in court, he said nothing about the victims in this case. Fatmir Limaj also suggests in his final brief that he acted responsibly as commander of the 121 Brigade with respect to the murders of Selman Binici and Ramiz Hoxha and the detention of the Serbian journalists. This is, in our submission, an extraordinary claim, for the Prosecution submits that the evidence shows just the opposite. Mr. Limaj tried to justify the Binici and Hoxha murders here in court with an obviously false story, and he admitted he did no investigation into the murders even though he was the commander of the area. With respect to the journalists, Mr. Limaj admit that had they were not given a trial as was represented to Human Rights Watch and that they were held for a month and a half, we submit, for no good reason. Both Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu also point to actions that they have taken since the war. In the respectful submission of the Prosecution, we say that these factors should not be considered as mitigating in this case. Following the war, Kosovo has been run with the help of the international community, and a proper attitude towards minority groups in Kosovo is therefore, one would expect, required of anybody in politics. Fatmir Limaj should not get credit for adopting this attitude after the war. Isak Musliu worked for a time in the police in Kosovo after the war, but was fired for lying on his application. The Prosecution has looked at other prison-camp cases that have been tried at the Tribunal, including the Omarska case, the Celebici case, and the Krnojelac case. It is very difficult to compare this case to those cases but it is clear that a critical factor in determining sentence is the degree of involvement that the accused had in the involvement of the crimes. In this case the Prosecution submits that all three accused were deeply and intimately involved in the operation of the camp which, it is important to say, was blatantly illegal in all respects. This is not a case of an otherwise legal detention centre where crimes occurred. Rather, it is a case of a camp that was illegal in every aspect of its existence. Because of the significant participation of the accused in this illegal camp, it is submitted that they should receive significant sentences. The Prosecution recommends a sentence of 20 years for Fatmir Limaj, 18 years for Haradin Bala, and 15 years for Isak Musliu. The lower recommendation for Isak Musliu primarily reflects the fact that he is charged with fewer counts in the indictment than the other accused. Although Haradin Bala was only a guard at Lapusnik, he should receive a significant sentence because of his direct participation in many of the crimes that occurred there. Although Fatmir Limaj did not directly participate in beatings or murders, he should receive a significant sentence because of his direct participation in the operation of the camp, his command role, his role in the Berisha murders, and the other aggravating circumstances which have been discussed. This brings to an end the submissions of the Prosecution. In closing, I will again return to something that Mr. Cayley said in his opening statement. He said that "The principal strength of the Prosecutor's case, Your Honours, is that the Prosecutor draws on evidence from multiple sources." In considering the evidence in this case, Your Honours, in evaluating whether witnesses have told the truth about Lapusnik and the accused or whether they have been mistaken, untruthful, or have exaggerated or minimised the evidence, we would urge the Court to look at the evidence as a whole and to look how the various pieces of evidence fit together in this case and corroborate one another. Of course there are some inconsistencies. That is to be expected in any case. And if the evidence were too perfect in this case and there weren't inconsistencies, then we or the witnesses would be accused of having manufactured the case. And of course it is true that there is no one single piece of evidence that is capable of telling the whole story, though there are some witnesses who tell much of it. But we submit that when all of the pieces of evidence are fit together from all of the different sources and all of these pieces of evidence are considered together, then it is our submission that a single essential story emerges about Lapusnik, about the prison there, and about the role of the three accused. We submit that the facts taken together show that the three accused were at the Lapusnik prison, knew what was happening there, played essential roles in the operation of the prison, sought to prevent the truth of the prison from coming out and, finally, are all guilty of the crimes with which they are charged in this indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm just going to arrange a little bit of furniture so there's a little bit more room. Am I visible? I think it may be a little difficult. And am I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'll put stereophonic sound. Your Honours -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can be seen and heard, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I realise it's a little difficult. I originally indicated and I'm going to keep to that undertaking that I would appreciate the opportunities of a day, in court time. I think he will be less than that, but the reason I mention it at the start is I have an unusual request to make, one that I would pose now so that you have time to consider whether it's one you might be able to grant when I finish, and I will obviously allow time if it's going to be granted, that there's no incursion on anybody else's following representations. But I would ask on behalf of Fatmir Limaj whether after I've finished he may be permitted to add a few words of his own. Now, I appreciate he has given evidence over a number of days. He also had a few words at the very beginning of the case after I opened it, if you may remember, on the same day. And if you were to allow that, he would not abuse that, plainly, and would not take more than -- I've asked him precisely how long he might take if he were allowed to address you further, and he said no more than 30 minutes, because I appreciate that he's perhaps not the best judge of how long he's going to be in his opening he was a considerable time and in his evidence some of his answers were extremely long. So I appreciate you're concerned about time. But as obviously this case is considerably significant not only for him but obviously for many others as well, he would ask for that. And if I may return to it after you've had a moment perhaps during the course of this afternoon or at a later stage to consider that, then I'll return to it. I don't ask for an indication at this stage. I have touched in asking for that request on really an extremely essential part of what we want to put before you, and that is the intrinsically important nature of this case and the intrinsically important nature of this Court's role in relation to this case. And if I may just quote from the beginning of a seminal work on Kosovo which I know many have read, Noel Malcolm's introduction. He originally wrote it in 1998, but he's updated it since. But the original introduction had some prophetic words and we say the prophesy made at that time had repercussions right through to this moment as I stand here now. What he said was: "The Yugoslav crisis began in Kosovo, and it will end in Kosovo." He puts that in quotations and he then goes on saying: "One can hear this repeated almost anywhere in the former Yugoslavia. It's one of the few things on which all the parties to the conflict of the 1990s seem to agree." So it is in fact suggesting, and we would adopt this, that Kosovo in one sense a crucible. And it being a crucible for that -- certainly that part of the world and obviously in this day and age with global politics as it is, the stability of that region has a knock-on effect in other regions. However, as you may have read over this summer in the press both here and in the United States of America and in -- and in England, there has been publicity given to the continuing difficulty in Kosovo, and a difficulty that, if I may just refer to what has been said although it's about said under the bracket of sentencing, namely that Fatmir Limaj's role was in a sense dictated by the international organisations after the war. I want to come back to that if I may, because we say that is a gross misstatement of his position. However, the situation has not been resolved by the international community, and one of the reasons it hasn't been resolved is of course the need for an internal leadership and an internal understanding of what is happening, and that has been the problem that has been publicised very recently, namely the United Nations and the United States of America have both commissioned an inquiry into, essentially, when it might be possible to finally even begin the process of final status. Now, you may think that this is a little distance from the case, but -- this case, but we say it isn't a little distance from this case, because as you're aware it was opened by the Prosecution, and we repeat it ourselves today and we also opened similar recognition that by the Statute and in fact in the information that is handed out as I speak today, in fact I have a copy of the information that's handed out to the public as they enter the building, about the objectives and the purposes of this court. It has a very special role, in fact, quite unlike a lot of other courts in the world, domestic and international. Some of the objectives, there are four set out in the general information sheet. They are well known to you but they are objectives that we say place this court in a very different category, and the reason why I mention it is it will require this court to apply particular principles in particular ways in order to satisfy the objectives. Now, the four objectives that are set out for the public who come here -- and this is very recent, it's updated on the 24th of June of this year: "Objectives. In harmony with the purpose of its founding resolution, the ICTY's mission is fourfold: To bring to justice persons allegedly responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law." Well, plainly a function that many courts have, and that is to bring people to justice. "To render justice to the victims." Again, a function that many domestic courts have. "To deter further crimes." Again, a function that many domestic courts have. But it's the fourth purpose which we say doesn't prevail over the rest but adds a dimension that makes the examination that we're going to make this afternoon in relation to final oral submissions in this case very significant. The objective is "to contribute to the restoration of peace by promoting reconciliation in the former Yugoslavia." Now, that function, that objective, we say, permeates not just the fact-finding liability role, in other words the satisfaction of the first three objectives. Of course it permeates through as has just been mentioned to the sentencing role as well. Plainly, reconciliation is something which is, as it were a hallmark, a criteria by which justice in this court is seen to be dispensed. And we say that is particularly important for the international public and for obviously others as well, but particularly since it's an international court. Because what people will be looking for, what everyone wants is to see how issues that need to be resolved, and of course that's the stage at which we are, how they are resolved in order to, as it were, satisfy those four objectives. And in doing that, we say, and that's why I'm going to come to not a repetition of our time brief with the paragraph numbers and all the rest of it, and I'm quite sure you've had an opportunity to see that; I don't wish to repeat that at all. What I wish to do is extrapolate and in a sense distil what the essential problems may be facing any international court with that burden placed on upon it, a burden which no doubt is properly and happily taken because of the objectives themselves. The law has to be very clear if the Court is going to perform that role. The law has to be clear not only obviously in the Statute form but how it's interpreted. And in particular, we say, there has to be an even-handedness, because if there isn't an even-handedness then the fourth objective isn't being achieved and it's lapsing into the very problem that is still persisting in Kosovo: a division, a serious division that has not yet been breached or has not yet been bridged in either sense of those terms. And of course the final matter which is important in even-handedness, which is a principle that I think every jurisdiction adheres to although they call it different things, whether it's a natural law of justice or some other term, and that is that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done, and that of course is particular important here. And in order to as it were transpose those observations and make them relevant to this case, we've selected three areas which I will deal with in a little more detail but not exactly the detail that is in the final brief, not the same detail in terms of repetition. The three areas are firstly -- and we say it is an extremely significant one here because it's a precursor to the jurisdictional issue, namely the question of armed conflict, which has been addressed most recently by the Prosecution. And secondly -- the second area which we say is significant here and probably poses one of the biggest difficulties - and I don't wish to preempt, of course, your approach to it - but it would appear to all of us that one of the biggest problems in this case it may be in others as well, and I don't speak for other cases, but certainly in this case is the category which I would term reliability. That is, reliability of the material upon which you are to pass judgement in order to come to conclusions about guilt according to the necessary standard of proof. And if the standard of proof is going to mean anything in any case, namely beyond reasonable doubt, and of course I don't address you further on that standard, it's a well known onus and a well-known standard. But it has to be borne in mind that one has to return to how reliable is the material that you've been provided with in this case upon which to found a verdict which if it is to be one of guilt has to be assure foundation. Because if it is anything less than a sure foundation, in fact none of the objection -- objectives are being achieved. And in this category as with armed conflict - we will see and we will certainly suggest that there is - and we hope of course that it will not be perpetrated by the Court itself, there is a duplicity in the way this case has not only been approached but also the way in which materials have been garnered and culled to put before you. The third area which I want to deal with as well is an area which interestingly the Prosecution didn't address at all in their final brief and didn't address before you until moments ago, and we say in this case above many others it will have a strong bearing. We open the case by indicating it might be the key to it, namely the very nature of the person, namely Fatmir Limaj, that you're dealing with here. In many cases perhaps looking at the character and personality may not be particularly relevant. So for example it may not be particularly relevant if you're dealing with an overwhelming case with independent, verifiable evidence about which there can be no doubt. But of course we say that's not this case, and that once you are therefore in a different arena in terms of the material you're dealing with, then you have to look at who is the person against whom these allegations are made. And if I may just for a moment, because with the words of that just been uttered by the Prosecution, I think it is appropriate for me to begin with a very strong rebuttal of the observations of that been made, albeit under the heading of sentencing, before I deal in a little more detail with the three areas. Because the suggestion is that Fatmir Limaj in some way or another is some sort of opportunist who has jumped on a bandwagon after -- as it were after the war was over and has only espoused principles because in a sense they have been forced on him. Nothing could be further from the truth. And I'm only going to summarise it for these purposes: You have heard from a large number of people, an unusually large number of people who we say of course will have a bearing if the sentencing stage is ever reached, but they have a bearing and will have a bearing on the third area, namely the assessment of Fatmir Limaj. This is not somebody who has, as it were, picked up a baton being carried by the international community and run with it. This is somebody who has put his position on the line at a very early stage. And if I may just deal with two citations at this stage in relation to what he's told you, because we say they're very important. One deals immediately with the Prosecution's suggestion, and we -- that he has as it were that he has only taken up these things after the war is over. There came a stage in his evidence and you may remember there was a long period of time when we showed a video that had been compiled and he narrated his way through it in order to give hopefully some assistance as to terrain and so forth. Once that video was over there comes a portion - if you need the reference from transcript point of view, it's T6052 - there then comes we say a very interesting and important narrative. I'm only going to read part of it, which illustrates clearly -- and none of this was challenged. The Prosecution in cross-examining - and they did it for long enough as you know, no complaint; but they had plenty of opportunity - if the suggestion was go to be as it is today that somehow Fatmir Limaj didn't really genuinely have these principles, did you hear a single question put to Fatmir Limaj on that basis? Not a single question. None of the, if I may call it, background, political, and intent material was questioned at all. None of the witnesses who came to support his position both just after the war and during the war, none of them were challenged on these issues, none of them, one being somebody I'll come back to right at the end, the mountain teacher. So it hardly behooves, it hardly behooves the Prosecution at this late stage to start making suggestions of this kind. And the passage which I asked him to deal with after the video, he says this, T6052: "I mention here that after I became a member of the General Staff," that was in the November of 1998. He then at a later stage deals with what happened in the following year, which was the massacre at the beginning of the year when 40 civilians were killed and the killing was condemned. There is only one witness in this case who hasn't been prepared to accept it and I think you all know which one that is, the witness who has now virtually been ditched by the Prosecution. However, in the wake of that, as described in Noel Malcolm's book and elsewhere and you may be aware of it, there was international pressure to, as it were, try and solve what was going on in Kosovo. And it was that massacre by the Serbs of 40 civilians that caused this. And it was the conference held at Rambouillet near Paris in France. "It is a public knowledge now, this fact,Fatmir Limaj said to you, that talks in Rambouillet went for two weeks but didn't end [sic] with the signing of a peaceful agreement because there were members of the units who were not yet clear about the importance of the agreement." They were unclear. "Of course this was the doing of certain persons. Therefore, they demanded that the Kosovo delegation return to Kosovo to make clear to the people the importance of this agreement." I pause. The significance here is that Fatmir Limaj is participating on behalf of the KLA in talks with the Serbs at a time when the Serbs when the Serbs were doing absolutely nothing on the international arena other than committing acts of murder and aggression themselves. You may therefore readily understand that as an Albanian for him to be participating in these talks and then returning to his community to persuade them to accept the result of the talks which were intended to be a deescalation of armed force in Kosovo and particularly the presence of the Serbs was an extremely important role. And this was happening during the war. This wasn't something that he therefore adopted after the war. And he said: "The decision to take part in this [sic] was the most important. I think this is where I played an unusual role regarding the participation in such a peaceful conversation [sic], which after all was our goal, to come to" -- some of it I think may have been mistranslated -- "to the face where we could solve once and for all the question of the status of Kosovo but as you know the Serbs refused to accept the agreement." And of course as you know, the fighting went on, certainly on behalf of the Serbs, and it was only brought to an end not by negotiation by the international community because unlike, unlike Fatmir Limaj, there were others around the table who were unwilling and in fact never intended probably to curb their ambitions on Kosovo, and it was only the NATO bombing that actually brought matters to a head rather than Rambouillet, but I mention it because that is an indication very clearly that he took a position at a very sensitive period in the war when in fact if he had been playing political games he wouldn't have done it. He wouldn't have wanted to be seen negotiating or agreeing anything with the Serbs. There is one other reference I mention at this time because it indicates, and I think the Tribunal itself has used the word -- the description at one or another time, and that is that truly Fatmir Limaj can be regarded by you as a statesman, not somebody who is a mere politician looking for support. And the list of people who -- I merely list them at the moment and I don't go through them in detail: Jan Kickert, Peter Bouckaert, Carolyn McCool, Dan Everts, the former Prime Minister, and of course finally the mountain teacher that you heard from. They all speak in extraordinarily glowing terms about the commitment of this man during the war as well as after the war. And this is what on another reference I give at transcript 6062, Fatmir Limaj said to you: "My political stance was known," and this was in answer to a question about his attitude towards ethnic minorities within Kosovo. "Now, I was a person who made my views publicly known as well as those of my party. Our position towards minority was clear. I have always stated during election campaigns and in rallies we have an example. We have an example of Milosevic, I have always said. If we want to have the same fate as Milosevic, who is a dictatorship state, then we know better than anyone what a state means, when you deprive people of their rights, when you... use violence against them. So for us we don't need a better example of not doing what we should not do. "The other alternative is the one that is presented to us by the international community. We are still a long way from civilised Europe and world and therefore we should undertake the steps to build a free society where every citizen should feel equally free. This is an objective we have for the future. It's not easy for us because the war left an imprint on a large number of us and the Serbs who had left Kosovo, some of them had been involved in the use of violent. And so after the entry of KFOR and the return of 700.000... from places or different places they returned" to Kosovo, "finding that their parents or children had died." And of course there was -- and he goes on to talk about the feeling of revenge that existed at that time, and I'll come back later to what attempts he made to placate and ameliorate the obvious feelings of revenge that might occur at such a moment in time. And that, if I may say, leads into the first area, namely armed conflict. Because once again not only does one have to look at the history and background of Fatmir Limaj himself, but one has to go back before starting to make assessments in this area to the history and context of what had happened before those three, four months in the spring of 1998. And we would certainly ask that you do not view it in isolation for the purposes of this indictment. It's relevant -- that is, the history is relevant, which I'm going to turn to in a moment; we opened some of it and there's a little in the final brief as well. It's important because in order to understand what did actually happen in 1998 and whether in fact what was going on could constitute an armed conflict, one has to see what was it that had occurred in the decade before 1998 that produced the activities that I'll come to in 1998 and whether therefore the Geneva Conventions and Common Article 3 should necessarily apply to it. There is another aspect to this, and the other aspect is what I mentioned at the beginning, is the seemingly duplicitous nature of the way in which the Office of the Prosecutor has approached these cases emanating from Kosovo and Serbia. So with that introduction, may I just go back a fraction to see what the order was to gauge the measure and size of the problem that was facing those people who lived in Kosovo in 1998. You may be aware and you may now remember that from 1987, the Serb authorities' attitude towards Kosovo was a clear and unadulterated and singular one. There's no doubt about this. This doesn't require evidence on both sides. Much of what I'm about to say in fact is derived from what is termed additional material in the indictments against Milosevic, the very case occurring in this court at the same time as this this morning. The policy, I'm going to term, is not a term that's used by the Prosecution in that case, but it is a term that is coined by others. It's a policy of mass terror after 1987, because it was in that year that Milosevic himself took advantage as an opportunist - quite unlike Fatmir Limaj - as an opportunist as it were of promoting his own position and profile. He was invited to go to Kosovo by his government at that time, others being unwilling to go. He'd never shown any interest in Kosovo before, but he made a speech on the 24th of April that was to make his career, and that is no doubt why many regard Kosovo historically and recently as being the crucible. And what he did on the 24th of April was to endorse the Serb nationalist agenda in Kosovo and made statements about the fact that, No one addressing the Serbs in Kosovo should ever beat you, were the words that were quoted. Thereafter, that's from 1987, virtually a decade through to 1998, it was continuous. It was consistent, and it was essentially ethnic cleansing as it turned out by 1998 and 1999, but it was a slow but oppressive process. In 1988, high-ranking Albanian figures were dismissed. In 1989, the Serbian Assembly started amending the Serbian constitution in order to strip Kosovo of its autonomy. The same happened in the following months until, as you may again remember, there was a time when the constitution effectively and the autonomy of Kosovo was revoked, which it had enjoyed since 1974. That happened in 1989. And then after that throughout the 1990s and early 1991, again all from the Milosevic indictment, thousands, it is said, of Kosovo Albanian doctors, teachers, professors, workers, police, civil servants were dismissed. There can be no other explanation than this was an attempt to eradicate the Kosovar Albanians, eradicate by forcing them to get out, because the possibility of life was going to be untenable. And you have heard about the denial of language rights, the apartheid right down to the use of lavatories, as to who should use what. Cultural and religious symbols were destroyed. Police violence against civilians including the use of torture. And we've had one torturer here. The Prosecution in this case felt still it was necessary, until it was pointed out very clearly that -- it would be suitable to call this individual, and we'll have to return to this. Suitable, why? Because you can believe some of what he says? Is this the standard to be applied? We haven't heard so much about him more recently, and it's not entirely clear what you're supposed to do with that individual. We would say dispose of him and rely on nothing that he says to you. So there is absolutely no doubt that the regime facing ordinary citizens in Kosovo was a horrendous one and it went on with the campaign of shelling Albanian towns, Albanian villages, Albanian farms, cattle, crops. Every means of employment, means of survival were slowly being destroyed. And the indictment in Milosevic suggests that the United Nations had estimated by mid-October 1998, so the year we're actually obviously interested in, over 298.000 people, roughly 15 per cent of the population, had been internally displaced. That's nothing compared with the figure they later quote by May of the following year 1999, the very year in which the Rambouillet conference had been assembled. Over 740.000 Kosovar Albanians, approximately one-third of the Kosovar Albanian population had been expelled from Kosovo. There had been Security Council Resolutions condemning the use of extensive force by the Serbs. And there had been a Resolution indicating that the situation, and this is in September of 1998, that the situation in Kosovo had deteriorated and constituted a threat to peace and security in the region. And it was because of that threat of course and the Holbrooke agreement that the OSCE-Kosovo Verification Mission was established. And one member of that mission - which I'll come back to in a moment, which you've heard very little about because of course it was disclosed late in this case on the basis that the Prosecution claim they didn't appreciate its relevance - (redacted) has provided you with an extraordinarily important and pertinent statement on this very issue of whether in fact there was an armed conflict. And the indictment in Milosevic then goes on to talk about Rambouillet and I've mentioned Fatmir Limaj's role in that. I pause for a moment in a situation where thousands have been displaced, hundreds of villages and homes have been destroyed. People have been killed. As you know, because one of the triggers, the Jashari family in the spring of 1998 is said to be the reason that people returned to Kosovo. What are the people of Kosovo to do against that background? Now, this is important in terms of the application of the Geneva Convention, because if I may just step back a moment from the -- for the purposes of this, it's all very well for the Prosecution to say as they do and emphasise that of course the ICRC are saying that the Convention and Common Article 3 has got to be applied as widely as possible. Well, that's a very empathetic, sympathetic gesture and it's very important plainly that the relationships of warring factions, of armed states are carefully controlled. However, it -- was intended, the conventions, as you know, to protect victims. That's what it was all about in the first place. Who were the victims of the history I've only given a very short synopsis of for that decade? I think there can be probably no issue. I would not imagine for a moment that the Prosecution in this case would say that Kosovar Albanian citizens and civilians had not been severely victimised in the way I've described. In the circumstances, therefore, that prevailed by the beginning of 1998, if those - and I posit this - if you were yourselves to live in a small village of the kind depicted on that video, fairly remote, fairly vulnerable, you don't have arms, all you have is the possibility of somebody in the village having a hunting rifle. But what you do have is a much stronger possibility - which the Prosecution accept, that the VJ and obviously Serbian police for that matter - but certainly authorities not only had a far greater propensity to use force but also had far greater resources. So the risk that the villagers were facing was the presence of armoured vehicles and of course eventually tanks. Which is of course, when shelling occurred it was clear that they had very little or no protection. If in those circumstances what happens in the early stages, and that is the spring of 1998, is that villagers themselves say, "Well, we have to protect what's left. Otherwise, there will be nothing." Are the groupings that occur in that way, and there is a consensus that that is what was going on, are these groupings, sometimes described as a horizontal association that are occurring organically, naturally erupting, are they to be characterised as parties to an armed conflict just because the other side, not because they need to eradicate terrorism but of course they - that is the Serb authorities - categorised the KLA and what was going on as terrorism. Interesting, that. They didn't themselves regard it as some for the of no doubt armed conflict. Not that that matters for your purposes what the Serbs thought or for that matter what anybody else thought about the matter, but that is in fact their approach. Their approach was to use this not even insurgency but this protective force as an excuse, labour it terrorist and then swarm in, which is of course what they began to do. And as Colonel Crosland said at one stage had they chosen, they could have wiped the KLA out overnight almost at one stage. So this was a situation where if you were abroad watching your homeland being destroyed almost in a war of attrition conducted by a heavily armed Serbian force, then it's hardly surprising that you might, one, want to come back and help, and we say this is not some act of opportunism by Fatmir Limaj or any of the others who came back. Think of it for one moment. If you had left Kosovo and you were in Switzerland, Italy, Sweden, wherever, how much easier would it be for you to say, "I'm not going back there. I'll let the others do the fighting"? So actually the mere fact of a return I would submit to you is a significant one, risking lives. And a lot of people died. Of that there is no doubt. And Fatmir's description to you and I'm not going to read it out, I'm merely going to describe it because you will remember it was a graphic description. People are coming back in small groups, crossing the border. Yes, arms are coming over the border because they have but few themselves, as I've mentioned the odd-hunting rifle here and there. There's no point coming back and saying to villagers, Well, just use your pitchforks when they come in. You only have to think across to Africa at the moment and what has happened in Darfur and elsewhere. Are people supposed to say No, no, no, it's all right, you can do what you want you can come through you can destroy all of us. All our existence can be destroyed and we'll just leave. Or are they to do what anybody I think would submit is a natural and legitimate aim, and that is to protect what little is left? And what Fatmir did effectively was to go to the area that he knew best. That's what they all did. There's no doubt about it. On the map you can see where he was born, where his family lived. That's where he went. He went to the villages nearby to -- of course it would be easy to say organise, but actually not; merely to raise the level of awareness that it is possible to withstand aggression. It's really racing morale. That's what's doing in the early stages. Whatever the KLA may have done in previous years starting in 1996, it could -- could be described and has been described as guerrilla tactics, hit-and-run tactics, targeting particular individuals or premises. But what was happening now is completely different. This wasn't a guerrilla operation, nor was it at this stage, that is the spring of 1998, the very period that you're dealing with in terms of whether there was an armed conflict was merely raising awareness and getting people -- as the Prosecution now say, Oh, well, digging a ditch, that's an organisation. That becomes somehow or another a manifestation of an army. Well, all I would suggest to you that digging ditches, yes, is a manifestation of protection. It's a manifestation of the need at least to save what you have left. And we submit, therefore, that this process, this organic process of which Fatmir Limaj played such an essential part - but so did others, he was one of many - each village no doubt deciding amongst themselves not because somebody back in Switzerland, some highfalutin figure who may or may not be on the General Staff says you've got to do it here you've got to -- it doesn't operate like that. It couldn't operate like that. It had to operate on a consensus basis of these people in the villages willing to do it. And of course by this stage they're beginning to realise that unless they do something there will be nothing left because the crops are being burnt and so on. That's what's going on. So when the words as they do crop up in various interviews, prior inconsistent statements and so on about coordination, cooperation, agreement, it is because this is a very different kind of situation, not the kind of situation that is commonly evoked or invoked in armed-conflict situations. It is where a group of people have decided effectively on self-help. I wonder -- I'm just looking at the time, whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have over ten minutes anyway, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Ten minutes. Yes, it certainly is. So the question then is having looked at the nature of this movement essentially -- and we say it's not insurgency. We say in fact whatever the Serbs may have thought about it isn't even terrorist. It is effectively a self-help protective force, if you want to use any term at all. Now, if the Common Article 3 and the convention is going to apply to this kind of force, then one has to be entirely clear what the criteria are before obligations are going to be imposed on what we suggest is a somewhat higgledy-piggledy arrangement of villages doing it themselves and no doubt attempting to have some kind of hierarchy but not essentially achieving it. And the two limbs as it were that have been suggested, and I'm obviously not undermining them but asking really how far they really take you. One is the intensity or the protractive nature which has elaborated yesterday and the other is organisation. To save time I'm going to concentrate on organisation and may I say so it's clear we have also, to shorten matters for you, a response on the question of armed conflict in writing. I'm note going to -- I think you may have already have it. I'm not sure. May I -- oh, you have. It's just on this first area, armed conflict. I make it clear I'm not going to read it out I'm not going to go through it in detail. It's merely there in a sense to shorten matters. Perhaps you'd be kind enough to read it at a later stage. However, one of the matters that we highlight in this skeleton is, of course, the threshold and extent of organisation. If the intensity of the conflict can and has to be looked at in a broad context geographically speaking, so one isn't just looking at what happened in and around Lapusnik, as the Prosecution have averred, but in other parts of Kosovo, the question I pose is: Does the same apply to the organisation in inverted commas of this protected force? And essentially the question is this: What is the threshold that has to be applied, and we say it's extremely important that the threshold is addressed, because otherwise once again in pursuing these objectives that have been set out in the Statute and the information and so on I've mentioned, there has to be a clear understanding who the conventions are aimed at and what kind of conflict they're going to as it were apply to. What triggers the conventions. And we say what's happened here is that the appearance of people occasionally in camouflage uniforms, the appearance of the hunting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rifle and even the odd machine-gun because there weren't too many of those, is then said to as it were -- and even perhaps the obtaining of arms across the border coming into Kosovo over this period of time, are they the -- are they the signs of organisation that therefore then make it applicable as widely as possible? The Prosecution really don't help. What they say is Oh, well, these criteria are not exhaustive. For example, banditry; short-lived, unorganised insurrection; terrorism. These are just possibly guidelines. Well, I don't dispute that. But then what is the threshold if that isn't? So for example, is organised terrorism caught by this? Because if it is - and I only say it in passing because I appreciate observations that the Tribunal have made in the past - if it is, then certain other organisations in the world that come well within it. The IRA, ETA and so and. Protracted, many years, dominate certain territory, plenty of weapons. Camouflage uniforms, discipline codes, all that kind of thing. Are they caught or are they not or is it arbitrary? And we say this is -- this is the kernel of this area. It cannot be arbitrary. There has to be a clear understanding and we say this case demonstrates the possibility here that what has happened is that the KLA have been, or rather these defendants as representing the KLA, have been characterised as an army for the purposes or the triggering of these provisions when in fact if you look at what was happening on the ground there was actually no organisation that gets anywhere near the sort of organisation that ought to trigger these -- these provisions. And if one needs -- perhaps I'd just refer to it at this stage and deal with it in a little detail afterwards, and I do want to as it were go through it because it's the statement of (redacted), but he was preceded by our own expert Mr. Churcher. Interestingly, both Churcher and Crosland who gave evidence for the Prosecution had experience in Ireland and as you may remember I asked Colonel Crosland quite a bit about the comparisons between the two and there are a lot, but I don't take that further at this stage. But so far as Mr. Churcher is concerned, he has provided you - it was DL13 - he provided a starting place, and at this point it has to be remembered that we did not know that the Prosecution had (redacted) (redacted). But in fact, we say what Mr. Churcher told you in evidence and what he put in his report in fact is reflected and echoed in (redacted) statement to the Prosecution. So leave aside what members of the KLA may or may not say, whether it's Fatmir Limaj or whether it's somebody called by the Prosecution. Leave aside all that. The people who have certainly an understanding of military matters have attempted to obviously survey the scene in Kosovo. And the nature of the military command is set out on the fourth page of DL13. And what he says under the nature of military command is this: "Through the testimony in this case it's come out time and again that the witnesses refer to discussing orders or accepting them. This cannot imply a military-command framework in a military sense. The fundamental difference between the creation of the KLA and other forces in the Balkan conflicts was that they had no military --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please slow down while reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: -- a command structure." Well, is he talking nonsense or is he not? And of course we called somebody who was in the KLA and concerned with attempting -- one of the few militarily trained officers who had actually served in Bosnia. And of course that happens to be the contrast that Mr. Churcher himself makes with what happened in Bosnia because he has particular experience of that. And of course one appreciates that the Prosecution do not have to show that the -- what was going on in the Protection Force in Kosovo was on the same level as a NATO army, but actually themselves, as I will demonstrate after the break, have not been clear as to what really was the description best fitting to this particular force. And just to continue with this particular paragraph on page 4 of DL13: "They relied on volunteers who did as they were asked if it suited them. There was no recourse to any real disciplinary measure other than taking one's weapon away or dismissing them from their group. This is not a system of military command that any militarily trained officer would recognise." And he gave in evidence as the graphic position whereby merely because you say you are in command and you give somebody a title doesn't mean to say that makes it an army of any kind or makes it an organisation in which on the ground there is an effective structure even of a rudimentary kind. And what we're suggesting here, there wasn't even a rudimentary structure which would begin to trigger, which would begin to trigger the provisions in the Geneva Conventions. And then he goes on to talk about: How do they communicate? I mean, it's pretty basic. How did they communicate? If I just stand back and ask you to reflect. What's the evidence? They had people running from one place to the next. The only way they went to the aid of other people is because Ah, we heard over the hill there was a bit of fighting going on. So what do the Prosecution say? If you run over the hill and join them on the other side, that's organisation. Somehow or another once again the protected force becomes elevated to something much grander than it really is. So Mr. Churcher, I'm not going through the rest of his evidence. We mention it in the final brief. But we say he's not to be dismissed. And plainly, if you are unable to dismiss him and this comes back to the onus and standard of proof, then one has to consider seriously (redacted). And may I, looking at the time, do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume at five past four.

utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, before you continue, the matter you raised with us at the beginning of your comments, we're disinclined to take the course you propose. utterances.text: We have prepared so it's a little easier to follow when it's a more detailed document, copies, hard copies, that is, of (redacted) statement. It's officially exhibited DL13, or part of DL13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm just check to go see if you have the copies. Yes, you do. (redacted). It is important to see on the first actual substantive page, page 2, in fact, what -- what and who he is. He's working currently -- it don't know whether he still is but certainly he was at the time of the statement, working in Kosovo as chief of operations the Min Action Coordination Centre. He's been an operations officer for the same organisation, he says, when he joined the army. But it's the next paragraph which puts him in a strong position in terms of the opinions that he later proffers. He's a qualified paratrooper, commando, combat diver, mountain leader, arctic warfare instructor, military ski instructor, small arms instructor and map-reading instructor. Then I go to the paragraph: "In October 1998." He was seconded to the Kosovo Verification Mission. That's the one I mentioned earlier after the Holbrooke agreement. "I received military briefings at South Cerney, which is in England. Those briefings included such things," and then he lists them. I mention that because it -- he's not as it were going fresh on this mission. And October 1998 is again a pertinent date because if the KLA, and we're dealing with armed conflict and organisation, was to be characterised as arriving at a threshold of organisation to trigger the Geneva Conventions, then surely they'd have reached it by October 1998, which is only two or three months after the period which you are specifically looking at. So we say it's very important period. And we also say, and I won't repeat it again but I mentioned it before the break, that it is remarkable that the Prosecution did not recognise the significance of this statement in time to certainly have it as part of much earlier stages of the case. However, we have it now. He says at the bottom of the page, "I was the operations officer for Kosovo." His responsibilities were management and coordination of the Kosovo field patrols. "I would task the patrols on a daily basis." Again, important for the purposes of the mission he was there. In other words, he was -- he had to have known what was going on on the ground in order to verify, for example, a reduction in hostilities, the nature of the hostilities, and whether either side is breaching the understanding, at least, post-Holbrooke. Then the next page he says at the top, "The primary purpose of the patrols at that time was to verify what actually was going on. The Serbs and the KLA would tell us certain things but they had to be verified" - so again he's not somebody who is just taking things at face value - "to ensure that the Holbrooke agreement was being adhered to. In effect, no one should have been shooting at each other. Had those terms were not being adhered to we had to find out who was responsible for the breach." And as time went on he became involved with liaison with the KLA. Then in the middle of this page is this important paragraph which has to be seen alongside Mr. Churcher's evidence. "On paper the KLA had a unified chain of command but in practice this was not the case. What can be termed as their General Staff had no credibility with their zone commanders. This is because the zones are determined by geographical features and the personalities within those regions had attained that status of authority by tangible activities on the ground and the KLA fighters were only loyal to their own zone commanders. The Albanian clan system has to be understood and recognised when dealing with matters such as this. The rank structure is determined by which is the dominant family." So once again, this is an echo of the description I gave in general terms of the way in which, rather like topsy, things were growing in the earlier months of the year from a guerrilla organisation to protective village groupings. That's plainly why the loyalty he describes there is very local. Everything's very local. And he says, "This would mean that decisions made by the KLA General Staff were not always agreed to by the zone commander and therefore, orders were not carried out." He gives an example. I won't trouble you with it. On the next page -- and of course by October there's no question on anybody's evidence there were zones. The question is how effective they were: "The zones were very insular and the method of operation by which zone differed dramatically and did not necessarily satisfy the needs of the other zones. "Even within the zones, there were individual factions who would not listen to the zone commanders. The zone commanders knew this, but they worked around it. "The General Staff of the KLA was set up in 1998 without any consultation with the zone commanders. This caused a great deal of indifference from the individual zones. They felt the members of the General Staff were not part of the group and had done nothing to be part of the group. They were set up to provide a recognisable and acceptable body of people for the international community to deal with." Very important observation. Again reflects entirely Krasniqi's role, for example, and the propaganda that was being put out in order to boost morale and possibly engage the internationality community's support. "The chain of command," he goes on, "on paper is General Staff, zone commanders and brigade commanders." And then he goes on to deal with logistical support. He deals with the Pashtrik zone, Drenica zone - I'm now on the next page - and the contact he had on a regular basis with teams who were living with the KLA. So they're inside the KLA as an observation team. And he says on page 6 at the top: "I would be in contact with my field officers on a daily basis to receive information from them and to update them on current developments... The tactical command in each zone was the responsibility of the individual zone commanders," and then he gives a particular example. In the next paragraph: "His response," that is, the commander Ramush, "was to say that his brigade commanders were responsible for their own areas and could take any action deemed necessary within those areas or these areas." Again, it is reflective of Mr. Churcher's observations on command structures. "All zones operated in quite different ways. Some commanders were reactionary. Some were more organised but it really depended on the personality who was in charge." Well, I think that alone doesn't really create an army in any sense -- oh, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Excuse me I'm sorry to interrupt. It's just that statement that's being referred to is in evidence under seal at the request of the witness, and I believe that that is not a problem except for the identity of the witness, and I would just ask if that -- if his identity which has been referred to on page 36, it may have been referred to before but certainly at page 36, if that could just be redacted.
