utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged. So I'd concentrated on all zones operated in quite different ways, and certainly I would suggest that that, given the way that the Prosecution are saying that the KLA have characteristics or features of an army, there is no army on earth that is run in this way. "The operations the KLA ran were more localised rather than being run on a national scale. They did have their ability to adjust their operations." Three guys are mentioned. I don't perhaps deal with that. Bottom of the page, something I mentioned before the break: "Orders between the zones were conveyed orally. There were very few written orders, but these were only issued in extreme circumstances," and then he deals with the NATO bombing. He doesn't know who organised the approach, but it wasn't very successful. And here we have another feature which I mentioned before the break, page 7 at the top: "The KLA had a runner system where people would physically deliver the orders whether they be oral or written." Further down the page: "A random sequential numbering system so number 1 wasn't the most important person." It's a minor detail but one wonders what exactly can be the character of this other than the organic ground-upwards situation, which is random. "I'm not aware if there is any system in place to acknowledge if the orders had been received. I'm not aware of any regulations or disciplinary regulations in force within the KLA. It was more the case of, mess up and suffer the consequences. If there are any in-house regulations they were enforced locally." He then gives an example which I don't go through. And then I'm going to end on this because it's a long statement and there's much more dealing with a much later period. But on page 8, the fourth paragraph down: "I cannot provide any information that would support the theory that the KLA this a command and control system in place. They were very fractious." We say, therefore, that statement derived by the efforts of the Prosecution, not the Defence, carries considerable weight because of the person who is making the observations, his background, his experience on the ground we say at a critical point. And therefore, we say -- may I just ask you to turn to the skeleton argument on the jurisdictional issue which we've submitted today just for the purposes of a couple of observations that link to that. This description that I've been elaborating upon of a ground upwards locally based situation in a sense is reflected by the inability of the Prosecution to as it were have a consistent description themselves. It's on page 3, and it's paragraph 8 under the heading "The Prosecution's shifting of the goal posts." And I merely here indicate that the description that the Prosecution have made of the KLA - it's just an indication, no more, that in fact our suggestions are correct - is they started off in their pre-trial brief suggesting that the KLA had a "well-organised structure." We say that was a nonsense. They then toned it down in their opening statement to a "rudimentary military structure" which functioned -- which functioned -- we say of course even that hadn't been reached. However, they upgraded it again in their final brief as resembling a fully organised army, having developed many of the characteristics of a fully organised army, using the phrasing. And most recently, of course, they've added to that by saying it doesn't have to be at the same level as a NATO force. But we say of course none of these descriptions fit what I've just read out, which is a fairly chaotic, and particularly so in the early stages, of people as it were running around trying to as it were gather up enough support to at least prevent the Serbs entering their villages. But there is another point we put in the next paragraph and that is of course: What's the start date for this armed conflict? Because whilst one doesn't expect precision in terms of a particular day, this is where one enters extremely interesting territory. The starting point in the indictment is no later than early 1998. There's nothing in the pre-trial brief about it. It's February or March in their opening address to you, and mid-May, that's through the expert Philip Coo, and there's nothing in the final brief, and there's nothing yesterday or today about what it's supposed to have started. And of course we say there's a very good reason for this. The reason is that the armed conflict hadn't begun at this stage because if it had, and if it was so clear that there was an armed conflict no later than early 1998, the big question that then has to be asked, with the bigger tapestry in mind and equal-handedness and even application of the law, is why on earth did the Milosevic indictment, which spent a lot of time - I've only culled some of it - on the incidents in 1998, in facts going back before that, back into the 1980s, where there was an opportunity for the Prosecution, the same prosecuting authority, to say there was an armed conflict which covered undoubted, we say, crimes committed by the Serbian regime during this period, 1998. So why not? Is this just a convenience? And we say this is another example where one has to look very carefully at this bigger picture before one starts, as it were, passing judgement on this case if in fact there is not an equality between cases that are actually going on in the same courtroom at the same time, as it were. Therefore, merely looking at the question of the date and the question of the Milosevic indictment where very serious crimes, we say far in excess of anything alleged in this case have apparently not merited the attention of the Prosecution for the purposes of this Tribunal, we say neither should what is alleged in this case attract your attention. Now, before leaving the skeleton, may I make clear, and I have done so over the adjournment because I don't want to take up necessary time about it. On page 5, it's the next page, there is a long section concerning the relevance of the Human Rights Watch conclusions which have been prayed in aid by the Prosecution both in their written final brief and in their observations most recently to you. We concede at once that the other organisations, there are three others, that are cited in this skeleton, and their conclusions are not reports that are before you. We were not intending that they should be before you. It was merely to indicate on the face of it that you should have no more recourse to Human Rights Watch for the purposes of determining armed conflict than having recourse to any of the other organisations; or, for that matter, American diplomats who characterise the KLA as terrorists. Other people's opinions, even the Serbian government's, on this issue is not definitive or even persuasive. And it is interesting in the Milosevic case itself when they came to issue, there isn't a decision suggesting that it should or shouldn't, in fact. The Tribunal on that case said they could continue without having regard to the Human Rights Watch conclusions. But if and as I understand it the Prosecution do object to that other material being before you, I'm not going to -- I'm not going to ask you to take up time as it were in a bywater of this case and therefore if it will satisfy certainly the desires of the Prosecution on this matter I'm happy that the matter is left and that you don't pay particular attention to those paragraphs. I hope that satisfies Mr. Whiting or perhaps it doesn't I don't know. But that's the best I can do at the moment. Otherwise, I don't take time on this skeleton and I leave for matters to be considered by you in due time. May I turn, therefore, from the question of armed conflict which we say precludes the jurisdiction to the next major topic of the three I had indicated I would develop. This next one is obviously quite a large one. I will endeavour to deal with it again without having to repeat everything that's in any of the final briefs for that matter, but it is significant because it requires everyone but particularly obviously yourselves to consider how best to assess material and material that in the end could be categorised to sufficiently satisfactory to provide a basis for a conclusion beyond reasonable doubt if there is to be a guilty verdict in any of these cases. And we say that the categories of material which you've been provided with do not -- do not provide or satisfy this test, because in each of the categories, and I'll go through them just to indicate the problems that are faced, there are severe shortcomings and deficiencies, and it's interesting that it's on the witnesses with whom there are severe shortcomings or deficiencies that the Prosecution most rely. Now, the categories of material or witness that we're having to look at under this heading are firstly witnesses who have been declared hostile, for which there have been applications and which you've granted, and in particular the repercussions of those applications, being the admission into evidence of prior inconsistent statements. I will come back to that. We we're not seeking to re-litigate as was suggested yesterday. But we do have observations, again in the context of the objectives of the Court and the particular function it has, and, we suggest, the very high standards that need to be applied not only to armed conflict but also to this area. So the first subcategory is hostile witnesses. The second category, there's really one person I've put in it and I'll refer to him only as Luan. I think everybody knows to whom I refer. And he's in a separate category because of his very particular position in this case, which also gives rise to, we say, severe problems. And then thirdly, there are the victim -- I'm going to call them victim-survivors if that's a satisfactory description. And there are a number of those, and again I'll indicate who they are. And of course what the Prosecution have done in their various stages of their final brief is to, in many of these cases, almost uncritically accept or ask you to accept as satisfactory material emanating from these various sources. And they go on particularly in their oral submissions yesterday to do something which those of us in common-law jurisdictions are very cautious about ever doing, and that is looking for corroboration from another of the what might be called tainted but at least deficient or flawed sources. And of course that's a nonsense, to start looking at corroboration from others. One has to look at each one individually to decide whether there's sufficient reliance that can be placed. And then of course if there can be sufficient reliance placed, you may then look at another witness and see whether there's sufficient reliance there. But what you don't do in order to decide whether the first witness is reliable is at the same time look at the second one and say, well he's saying the same thing so the first one must be reliable. It's a circular process of corroboration, we say. It may sometimes be embraced by domestic jurisdictions although we would suggest rarely, but at this level this exercise that has been engaged in here is one to be we say have one's face set against. And this is if I may take the first of these categories, the hostile witnesses. Because it does give rise if I may put it to you with a very important approach, and what I intend to describe here is really the conundrum, the problem being set in relation not to hostile witnesses but all witnesses in this case. Because what the Prosecution have asked you to do eventually and essentially is Well, all right there might be witnesses who've lied. I'm putting it in the short form. There might be witnesses who've lied, but nevertheless you're quite entitled to accommodate those lies, perhaps even overlook those lies on the basis that other things they're saying, same witnesses, can be used by you to provide material to support the Prosecution's case. That's putting it in a nutshell. That theme arises throughout many of these witnesses. Because some of them plainly -- for example, some of the victim witnesses, one we will suggest has lied in court but there are others who are seriously in error and confused. And once again we say you have to -- once you have a situation of either lies or serious confusion, you have to ask some fairly fundamental questions about whether it is desirable in the international arena for decisions and verdicts of this gravity in the context of the situation I've already described to bring back verdicts certainly of conviction to the -- to the level of satisfaction when you are dealing with a cherry-picking exercise, because that's what it is. Now, I'm in the asking -- I'm specific about this. I'm not going back and asking for all the arguments that we put to you, and we've mentioned them in the final brief. We've already done it in writing. You have them. You've ruled on them. But at this stage they do have a further bearing. And in relation to the hostile witnesses who come at the beginning of the analysis as the first category, what you said in relation to this issue at paragraph 29 was, firstly, that oral evidence remains the primary and normal standard. And we would accept that, because there is no point essentially in having in facility if at the end of the day not quite as a matter of course but as an increasing incursion on that, and you relate that in the second part of this paragraph, it is not the intended purport of this decision that an earlier account or statement of a witness should be admitted in evidence as of course at the instance of the party calling the witness to give evidence. But there is, we say, redolent in the approach of the Prosecution a risk that that is what is increasingly happening in these courts. And we say that it may be a difficult situation being faced by the Prosecution and the Court, but it is in these situations that the test of reliable evidence has to be even stricter than it might be in a domestic court. And that is why we say the standards of international justice, if anything, have to be higher. And of course you went on to say at paragraph 33, which is why I'm asking you to consider a general approach to evidence, because essentially what our submission comes to is this: If you decide in any particular case that is a witness has seriously lied and in some sense - not about anything, because plainly if he's lied about the colour of his socks or something that is peripheral or irrelevant, that may not matter - but has lied about a central matter, then you may wonder or you may consider whether it is sensible to go on and say never mind all that. We'll just look and see whether - this is what the Prosecution do - whether in fact this witness has said and I deal with command structure or whatever it happens to be, that Fatmir Limaj was at the centre of a particular structure in the Pashtrik zone or wherever it happens to be. And we say it's that jump, that leap from saying we can as it were accommodate the lies or the confusion that in this situation we say requires a much more strict scrutiny, and we say in the end that many of these witnesses, if you decide they have lied, then you do not go on to then say, well, we want to assess their prior, dealing with hostile witnesses, their prior inconsistent statements. And this is really related to paragraph 33 where you say: "It will be for the Chamber to determine what weight if any it will eventually attach to either or both of these video recordings" - that's of the two hostile witnesses I'm about to touch upon - "when it comes to assess all the evidence at the final stage of the trial." And you do indicate that will demand the most careful scrutiny of the Chamber. Well, it is in that context, namely the careful scrutiny of the Chamber, that we suggest in the hostile category for example that the careful scrutiny in the end should result in prior testimony not supplanting or substituting actual testimony. Whatever may be the intentions of the Prosecution, it is oral evidence that should at the end of the day in an exercise of this kind be dominant, and if you feel that the current oral testimony is lies, then we say it's so significant. And because the conditions under which previous statements were taken are, we say, particularly, if I take the Shukri Buja statement in context first as an example, and I'll move on to Behluli. What you have to recall is that if you're going to use the prior statement to supplant effectively what's been said in evidence, then you have to look at how the prior statement was taken and the circumstances under which it was taken. One of the most obvious observations here, and it will apply to many of these cases, is that once a person knows that there is an investigation into war crimes in an area in which the person himself or herself has exercised authority, what do you imagine goes through the mind of that person? That -- even if they're not summonsed as a suspect, even if they're not charged with anything, they are going to be concerned about their position and the potential risks that they're facing once they realise that is the position. Plainly, that applies to Shukri Buja. In fact, he was told during his prior interview at one point that his name had come up. So he was aware not just that this was an investigation into war crimes but that his name had come up. And plainly he's not going to be asked questions because he hasn't got anything relevant to say. And therefore one's going to do the process of assessment about how much store you set of an interview conducted in those circumstances when -- if you've already decided or begun the process of deciding that his current testimony is a pack of lies. If his current testimony is a pack of lies, then you have to reflect on whether what he was saying in a prior interview may also be the same but for different reasons. But in any event, of course this does give rise once again to the issue which we've highlighted in the final brief, but it's a good example, a system known as proofing, because if you're going to make assessments about prior inconsistent statements, you need to know how do the changes come about. Well, as you know in this particular case and in a number of others, the process by which witnesses are proofed is not recorded as such. You don't have a formal record let alone a video record of what actually happened here in this particular case when he came or was about to give evidence on this matter. But this isn't the only case where the material is lacking. In other words, what has brought about the change? It's surmise by the Prosecution what has brought about the change, because their case is he told the truth in the prior inconsistent statement, airbrushing out Fatmir Limaj, as they were putting it on one occasion. But what happened here was that the information that we got, that is the Defence, came one day before he gave his evidence, and it was very short indeed. It merely indicated that he was not -- not going to be in a position to say that the structure of the KLA was as described in the prior interview and that Fatmir Limaj was not his commander. That's all it said. Well, that's very interesting, but of course it don't tell us much as to how that's come about or why he should be doing that. And of course the letter that was sent of which you saw a part at one stage indicated, and we've put it in the final brief as well, that they knew -- the Prosecution knew full well because of the proofing that he wasn't going to say that he'd said before or at least they thought he wasn't going to say the same as what he said before. And it's very important, because it goes right to the heart of the very point that you make in your ruling about are we slowly sliding towards a situation in which the Prosecution essentially is just going to call anyone who is relevant in their eyes even if what they're about to say in their view isn't the truth according to them, because their view is there was a KLA structure and Fatmir Limaj was at the centre of it and so on. And what they said in the letter of the 14th of March, this is after he has been called, this year, it's these words: "It was our immediate impression that he was aware of what he had said in his OTP interview, that he intended to depart from what he had previously stated and was anxious about being confronted with his OTP interview in court." Well, in -- we would submit in proper circumstances what ought to happen on these occasions, firstly, there should be a proper record of what exactly is transpiring between a Prosecution that have a very clear picture of what they want to establish and a critical witness that they now rely on none of his evidence but all of what he said in his prior inconsistent statement. Nothing could be clearer than an attempt here - because they knew full well they were going to almost certainly, almost certainly request that he be treated as hostile - is this very exercise we say there should be a sanction on this sort of exercise. The sanction is if you're going to call a witness who in most jurisdictions, certainly those of us who represent parties, are not supposed to call witnesses who we do not believe are going to tell the truth, is that going to be the standard here that a party is entitled to call a witness who they don't think is going to tell the truth and then say to the Tribunal, "You sort it out"? You have then the obligation to as it were We're going to throw it up like confetti and see where it lands and you take the bits you want and the bits you don't want. Which is why we say this is a cherry-picking exercise of some magnitude. And what happened here should never have happened. They shouldn't have called him at all. You wouldn't have been deprived of the truth through him because we say it is now almost impossible to tell what the truth is in his case. And I'm afraid we're going to have to look at the interview in a moment. But before we do, there is one further feature in this case, in Shukri Buja's case, that is very important. If the question that you're being asked to decide - we say you shouldn't have to decide and if it's going to continue in this way then you should put a marker down that this is not a satisfactory process - but if you're going to -- enter into that arena looking at what he said before, may I just remind you of what he had said before. And of course it's triggered in the interview with him. The OTP had already used this witness before. They used him, as you may recall, in the Milosevic trial as a Prosecution witness in order to deal with not just the events of 1999. In fact that is what he said in evidence he dealt with. But he provided a statement, and one of his objections in this case was that what happened then at the hands of the OTP was quite different to what happened here. On this occasion in 2001 - again, you've heard this material - he was interviewed over a number of days. He was provided with the record of that which he could see, and he signed it. And he imagined the same process was going to happen on this occasion. In fact it didn't. As you know, it was a video recording and there's controversy as to whether he could open the CD or he couldn't. But in any event leaving all that to one side, what did he say in the statement that he provided for the OTP in relation to the Milosevic trial? In fact, he was dealing with his arrival in 1998. He was dealing with who he came with. He was dealing with command structures. He mentions Fatmir Limaj and so on. And as I asked him in cross-examination, he was able to give the seven zones with the areas of responsibility, the zone commanders, and so on. All of that before we ever get to 1999. It is specifically, and I can give page references, I know it's not an exhibit itself, but the material within this statement is before you. What he said in the Milosevic statement is entirely consistent with what he is now saying in this case about the command structure or lack of it in relation to this period of time, 1998. So before you decide that you would rely on the video recording, if you're going to, you have to remember that before that he made a statement which is inconsistent. So what do you do? Choose the one in Milosevic because -- or not. Or decide, well, no, we won't use that one because in fact he was giving the evidence for a different purpose. Is therefore the truth to be decided on the purpose for which you give the evidence? I think not. The decision about the reliability of a witness cannot depend upon that kind of criteria. Now, what I would ask to happen, I'm sorry it's a slightly detailed exercise, but in view of the way the Prosecution are in fact asking you to rely, we say not to rely, on the previous statement, could I ask you to look finally at parts of what he said. Now, you will recall that I originally addressed you about some of this, and some of it's in the final brief. And with the Prosecution's kind help if we could have -- it's exhibit P160 and I just want to go back to some pages before the ones that are referred to in the final briefs. It's page 22. If that could come up on the Sanction please. It's page 22 at the bottom. I just want to go through this because you will see at once. Now, if it could be enlarged so it's easier to read at the bottom of the page. It should be "You mentioned in your earlier statement." I don't know whether that's easier to read. Yes. "You mentioned in your earlier statement." There. If that could be enlarged. Now, this is in fact a reference to the statement he gave to the Tribunal in relation to Milosevic. It's not spelt out but that's what it is. And the whole question is: How much reliance are you going to place on this interview? Even if you do look at it and decide that is your function is to pick your way through it and decide this is a satisfactory basis, because we will see -- think you will see. It's rather like the sea. It shifts. The meanings are not entirely clear, and it's not a situation, we say, that even this interview and I don't want to take it out of context; of course you will read eventually once again no doubt the whole of this video-recorded interview. He is dealing therefore with a time when Fatmir was the leader the unit that entered Kosovo. Then at that time were specific duties assigned to him. You see that's the next question, "particular or specific duties." So for DB read investigator. "SB: No, no. Until we arrived in Drenica there were no specific duties for us, that is for those in the group... After we arrived in Drenica, then Fatmir Limaj was appointed... to lead the unit." Now that's what he says there but you will in fact see what he means or perhaps what he means by that at the top of the next page, 23. Perhaps we could have page 23, please, top half enlarged.

utterances.text: If it's too difficult, I'll... Ah, thank you. The same is going to apply to successive pages, I hope, but if gets too complicated I'll carry on without it because the points are very simple. At the top of page 23, he continues: "That is, in fact Fatmir Limaj led the unit... errr... until we arrived at Klecka... and I have always counted him as my first commander on this basis. "When you arrived in Drenica, were you still together as a group," and so on; he says "Yes." Then a little further down he's describing what I have in fact already described today. So there is an interpretation of the whole of this interview, we say, that's akin to the description I've put to you of an organically growing organisation that is really a protective one. He says further down "Perhaps in Drenica, in fact in the villages where we saw KLA soldiers... we spread out among the houses... We stayed here. I don't know, several days. We were given the order, that is, to leave and to organise in the area as it was then called." He then deals with the various areas on the rest of that page. At the bottom of the page he is asked who gave the order. "Who issued the order that you had to go to these other areas?" Now, I'm turning to the next page. If there's equal difficulty about this next page, 24, I'll just carry on for the moment. What he actually said on the next page was: "We did not know who issued the order, but in fact the order was conveyed... by Hashim Thaqi." Now, there is then a question and an answer which we say is very important: "Did Hashim Thaqi mention to you the fact --" thank you. I'm just at the top of that page. It's important because if it is to be said this is not -- this is an interview and we say it's very common in these interviews. It's clear what the questioner has in mind. It's clear in a sense what the Prosecution theory is because here it comes out and it's sometimes quite subtle. "Hashim Thaqi mentioned to you the fact that Fatmir Limaj would be commander of this unit that was to go to... that area." The answer is no, not yes: "But we in fact knew Fatmir Limaj to be the most competent person because he knew the lie of the land." So when he says on the previous page I've always counted him as my commander, the counting him always the commander is because he was the most competent person because he knew the lie of the land. Is this really going to be used to indicate the kind of structure and the kind of command that the Prosecution require for this indictment? And then it's "Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work." Well as we saw in the expert's reports, coordination is not quite the same as having a command structure in the way that Mr. Churcher and others have described it. "While I had to coordinate with Fatmir... That is in fact how the organisation would work because there'd not been any organisation for some time." Well, we agree. "That is, any organisation of units. And information had to be brought to Fatmir, and then from Fatmir to the General Staff, and they we could then come back to us with what we had to do next." "This task that was assigned, that is assigning Fatmir as leader of the unit and appointing you to go to an area... were you given the task of staying there?" Well, that isn't exactly what he'd said but never mind. "Were you giving the task of staying there? Were you to set up a base, were you to start to organise yourselves... whatever kind of organisation was possible?" "Fatmir Limaj was appointed to go and set up in Klecka, in the village of Klecka." "And in fact... that... we were organising there." And they top of the next page 25: "That is in fact at that time ... they could not order us to 'go here, go there,' because they could not know where we could go, but we decided to which houses I could go and where I would be safe and where I could start organising." This is precisely in line we say with the organic growth of a protective force. "So," says the questioner, "you had a kind of priority in deciding as you judged yourself and then... you would decide where..." "Buja: We were independent to decide where to set up, that is in which family." Precisely the point that (redacted) makes because we could not know all the families. And then the rest of that page he's dealing with matters related to that. But I turn to page 26. The questioner at the top of 26 goes back to the question of assignments that you mentioned. Now, it means that each person was assigned top a certain area. These air assignments were given out by Thaqi and Drenica. And then he's given this answer: "In fact guidelines were not made in the form of orders because there was no... but we were told we were to go, that is where we were given an area, but we went there because there was no organisation." And then he deals with reporting back to Fatmir on that page. And then he says further down: "When I returned, that is in fact... in the beginning, there wasn't at Klecka but three soldiers went, and stopped in another place." And at the bottom of the page he's saying in fact, "When we arrived in Klecka that is there were only two of us. There was myself," and he names someone else. Now, these are all pages which -- I won't go through the rest at this stage, but they eventually lead to the passages which originally are in the final brief where he emphasises against and perhaps I could just come to page -- if we could go to page 32. On that page 32 he's dealing with the absence of a headquarters. He's dealing with small units of ten soldiers. He repeats in the organisational sense there was no headquarters. "It was called a headquarters but we didn't function as a headquarters. People came and registered, signed up as KLA soldiers," and so on. It's all a description of something quite different from the one that the Prosecution was striving for. And of course this is very close to the position on the next page where we have the suggestions, as we say, and the pressure being put on him to come up with a structure and to come up with what effectively has become the basis of the Prosecution case, because on 34 at the top -- in fact it's a continuation of what has happened on 33, but if we could have 34 at the top. The questioner is anxious to find out the organisation of the digging of trenches, and then at the top of 34 he says effectively this is the questioner but: "Regardless of the question of whether there was fighting or not, I would like to emphasise ... the moment when there was a kind of structure in that zone in that sense, I mean. In April 1998 there were regular weekly meetings at Klecka." And this is the questioner saying "as far as I know." There isn't were there; we say there were. "Did you take part in these regular weekly meetings?" Answer isn't yes because he's supposed to be coordinating with Fatmir. The answer is "No, because I wasn't part of the command of Klecka. There were special" -- sometimes the words have been misinterpreted, but "There were special occasions on which I did take part." He instances one in May. And then he -- further down the page at the same time: "When I was, that is in -- in the area of Kroimire I helped. At that time you could not. We had not even defined companies or battalions, only had posts. I helped, that is to survey positions, trench, bunkers and other things. And I had a support from Fatmir or... errr... the General Staff." And we get to a passage here which is quite remarkable since the Prosecution say you can rely on this because what he is saying is: "I thought Fatmir was a member of the General Staff and also most people thought that I was a member of the General Staff." Well, you can see straightaway that the conditions under which both they were operating at the time and certainly within this interview that he is plainly wrong about his perceptions and there was a time in the cross-examination -- in the examination-in-chief where I objected to some of the questions being put when it's not entirely clear the basis on which he had his information. And it's on page 36 - I don't ask for it to be put up. It's referred to in the final brief - when over and over again the investigator is asking the same question about the elementary structure and the diagram that is drawn we say is a nonsense. In other words, that it's putting Celiku as essentially just below the General Staff with all these other points around. Now, I'm just going to ask one rhetorical question. If any of this makes sense, then why when the zones were established in June, July, and on into the autumn, if he had, that is Fatmir had, as is supposedly described or hinted at here some -- in the diagram a position of command at Klecka over the region, why wasn't he made the zone commander? That would be the obvious thing. He'd be zone commander at that point. And the structure that they've got which is effectively -- there are two zones on this structure because there's the Nerodimlje zone on the right-hand side and the Pashtrik zone on the left-hand side. We say in fact that's not how it worked at all, and it is erroneous to establish Limaj in that way at the centre or core of the whole of this. So these diagrams and these answers that he's given in this interview which is a fairly lengthy one - and I'm not going to go through the rest; we've itemised the parts of it where it's clear he is in error - he's in error originally about his perceptions, but in fact one has to ask the question whether the description he really was giving is in fact consistent with the description that Fatmir Limaj is giving of people going to the areas they know best, setting up where they know best and asking people who they can trust. And you will remember that part of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the exercise was that one man is responsible for the next man. In other words, you only bring in people who you can trust. So it's organised horizontally, not vertically in the way that that is suggested. So we do say that these -- of course principally, we say, he can be forgotten, because effectively if he's going to be regarded as telling a pack of lies here in -- to you, and we say without the as it were due-process guarantees let alone the kind of measures that are taken in civil jurisdictions whereby the whole matter is governed by a judicial process from the beginning and isn't in the hands of one of the parties, then without that it's entirely unclear what the pressures must have been. But in any event, one has to go back to his original Milosevic statement, by which I mean the statement he provided in the Milosevic case. Now, in the same breath, if I may just deal with the other hostile witness I can deal with it hopefully not in quite such detail, but there are some interesting answers here which again are nonsensical. This particular witness, Behluli, is described in the final submissions by the Prosecution as being someone who is very careful about what he said. But once you begin to look at this witness you will see that is far from the case. Can I just read the bottom of the previous page to save coming up. This is what he's saying: "In the beginning because of the very limited numbers there were not such things as battalions. Supply of weapons grew the number of -- well, concerning April 1998 there was here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you please slow down when reading. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Speaking 1998. In Klecka there was general headquarters but with the time passing there were other points. UCK. They were all UCK points sets up. As the number of people, UCK numbers grew so they set up as more people came in and joined." Nothing remarkable in any of that. And then there's a further translation underneath and you will remember how these came about. But then the investigator says okay, but let's start with: "Can you tell me at this time in April-May 1998 what area was that area -- was in Kroimire was the responsibility of" -- Well, what I think he's saying or trying to say is whose responsibility was Kroimire. And he says the Pashtrik zone and then he says what it covers. Then he bit further down on the same page: "Well, it wasn't generally a common knowledge that there was such a thing as the Pashtrik operational zone. In fact, of course, certainly in April-May 1998 the zone wasn't in existence. But then everybody knew what the Kroimire was supposed to cover. Probably somebody hired up Luan or Shukri. They knew something and maybe this was in the paper that was as Pashtrik operational zone. But once we get this name Pashtrik operational zone," which is later, "then I come to know about the Pashtrik operational zone." Now, the question is: Did he come to know about the zone and what does he say about it? And he deals with the protection on that page. Could we then go to page 21, please. And then he says and he's dealing still with the Pashtrik zone and responsibilities, he's saying --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Top of the page: "Shukri Buja must be the most important person about it. I know that we cooperated with them. "Okay. Where was the -- the General headquarters for the area? We can now call it the Pashtrik operational zone." And he, that is the witness, says: "You are talking about 1998." "Yeah, still talking about the spring of 1998." He says, "The General Staff was in Klecka." "Q. In Klecka?" "Yes, in Klecka. Fatmir Limaj was there, the commander of this zone." It's complete nonsense. As you know. He wasn't the commander of the Pashtrik zone which didn't exist at that time anyway. And there wasn't a general headquarters in Klecka for that area. He - that is, Limaj - was in Klecka, as you know. I appreciate that is what the Prosecution would obviously like to end up with. And he says: "Yes, the general headquarters was located in Klecka." Okay. And he repeats: "Fatmir Limaj was the zone commander." Fatmir Limaj not only wasn't on the General Staff, which was one of the problems we've already encountered, he wasn't even the zone commander. "Okay. Was this already when you joined in April of 1998? Was it clear to you that headquarters in Klecka?" Then he says "No." "Okay. When -- when -- when -- when did you learn about this bigger -- bigger or uh like general organisation of the KLA, general organisation in this zone." And then he deals with coming to know about it later. And at the bottom of the page as regards the organisation, "It was here. I heard later that the General Staff was in Klecka." And on page 22, and I'll end with this particular one, he repeats the same, we say, errors and they are substantial if you're going to rely on this as a basis for determining command structure, armed conflict and so on. Towards the bottom of page 22, having dealt with the numbers of soldiers increasing, "Do you have any idea at this time who was the supreme? Was there a Supreme Command of the KLA in Kosovo?" So you can see again what they're striving for and the witness must understand what they're after. So he says, "Yeah, as far as I -- for the Pashtrik zone is concerned I know very well that Fatmir Limaj was the commander." Now I pause for a moment to try and be realistic about this. So what is the Prosecution saying? You can forget the lies in court; we can just rely on this interview. But actually, that we don't rely on. So that that isn't accurate. He's got it completely wrong. So once again we say it's the cherry-picking exercise even at that level as to whether this is a reliable interview even on the detail. And therefore we submit that in these two cases not only are they both being regarded as hostile and therefore we say the previous inconsistent statement should bear little or no weight, the question that you set in the ruling, but in any event if you start looking at it you can start recognising what the inconsistencies are and what the plain errors in relation to that. Another example, we say - moving from hostile witnesses. I indicated he is in a category of his own. I can deal with it quite quickly - is Luan. Now, if there is any cherry-picking in this case this provides the classic example, because in this instance this particular individual has been accused by no less than six different witnesses. I'm not going to read out their names. They're in the brief. One of them, however, is L-96, who is of particular relevance in relation to observations about Fatmir Limaj. And essentially we describe him in our final brief, that is Luan, that if these witnesses are dealing the truth about Luan, he is a the gate-keeper, basically. He is the man according to them who is absolutely essential and crucial in kidnapping people and for that matter interrogating some of them before they're brought from Kroimire, his area, to Lapusnik. What's the Prosecution's position on this? You might have thought that they would have worked this out before he was called. We say in a situation such as this, rather like hostile witnesses who they almost certainly anticipated would be, this is a witness who should have had his status determined such that when he was called it was clear to everybody the basis on which he was being called. Because there are cases plainly and Your Honours will be aware of them in domestic jurisdictions where somebody may for example do a deal in a common-law jurisdiction turn Queen's evidence and so on, as it's called sometimes. But in any event the meaning is clear. In other words, if you come and help us and accept your responsibility, it's possible that your sentence won't be as severe or there may be other benefits. And it's all sorted so everybody knows. To not sort this one we say is an abrogation of responsibility. So what the Prosecution really are doing is saying once again no, no, no. It's not us it's over to you. You sort this one out. Because the remarkable thing is when he was asked in his evidence about these matters, these allegations, he denied them in chief. What did the Prosecution do? Did they ask to treat him as hostile because he wasn't telling the truth? These are not peripheral matters. We're not down to the colour of somebody's socks here. We're dealing with -- we're back into dealing with central allegations in this case, the very allegations you're dealing with in relation to Fatmir Limaj. No, it would appear because there's no other interpretation and of course this isn't dealt with by the Prosecution satisfactorily at all other than to say oh, well, yes, well, he may have been alleged to have done these things but just overlook them when it comes to you know his own involvement in everything and rely on everything he says about other people. Well I think in everyday life you would be very dubious about doing that. If you knew that somebody you were talking to was telling you lies about themselves in order to protect themselves, you would rely on their word when they start talking about you or talking about someone else, neighbours your close friends? I don't think so. So the Prosecution appear to accept his denial. They don't challenge it. There's no sanction against this man. He's not charged, nothing. Not sitting in the dock behind me. Why not? Inconvenient? This Tribunal, we say, should not be governed by convenience. And should not be asked to govern by convenience. And we say once again, between like a hostile witness and we're going to put it shortly in this case. Once you have decided that somebody is seriously lying to you here in this courtroom, rather like a hostile witness is, that's an end of it. No going on and deciding Well, we'll look at what he says about the command structure. We'll look at what he says about Fatmir Limaj. Because once again the Prosecution are saying, well, he hasn't blamed anybody else. Too clever for that. The position with this witness is, as I've indicated with others, he didn't realise he might be in the frame when he's being questioned? He didn't realise there might and problem later on? He didn't realise it might be important to set up someone else in authority in case the buck stopped with him? So you can begin to see how undesirable it would be for this man to be elevated in any sense to start providing corroboration for either of the two hostile witnesses or for the hostile witnesses to be providing corroboration for him. May I turn to the question, therefore, the third category of material being used by the Prosecution. And I start with and here of course there will be hieroglyphics being used. L-64. I just pause. L-64. What were the Prosecution doing calling L-64 at all? He's almost but not quite in the same category always the other witness I've mentioned who the Prosecution have virtually ditched now. There could not be a more disreputable, dishonest witness than this one. You may recall, I'm sorry it took some time that I cross-examined L-64 for a considerable period of time, because there's almost no criminal activity that he hadn't been engaged in one way or another, well before he ever supposedly told the truth about this case. I mentioned just some of them. You will probably remember the high points; his own drug addiction; His drug dealing; his arms dealing; what was found on his premises; and the -- I suppose the high-water mark, certainly for judging whether this is a man whose word bears any relationship to the truth, is the finding of a certain quantity of powdered material otherwise known as heroin. What was his explanation? It's almost like blaming your grandmother. He said no fertiliser to you. That's what it was. Oh, I think it came to Canada. This is a man who will say anything to get himself out of what he perceives to be a troublesome situation. He's summoned as a suspect for the questioning. So his antennae must have been six feet out of his head realising -- because by that stage, locked up he may not have been, but the risk he was at, given that as you know now he had involved his family or at least his family were involved in certainly the drug side of it and also allegations of violence towards a member of his family. So here is a man who really engages in a series of activities that put him beyond the pale. And if up need corroboration for essentially a dearth of truth in this man's account you only have to look at his diary. Now, his diary is P169. His diary is used by the Prosecution no less than -- I've counted at least eight times in their final brief. Paragraphs 45, 53, 56, 60, 63, 69, 93 and 110. Very interesting that the diary is used because you have to then consider if the diary is being used to support this witness, what's the most obvious thing you would expect to be mentioned in this diary of important and significant events in 1998 that he's supposed to taken part in? An alleged prison camp in Lapusnik. He hasn't really got explanations for some of these omissions. They're rather glaring. As far as Fatmir Limaj is concerned, the most glaring omission which goes to the heart of what the Prosecution are saying against Fatmir Limaj is that in some way or another on the 15th of May is the suggestion that Fatmir Limaj acknowledged at a ceremony in Lapusnik that he, Fatmir Limaj, was effectively in charge of the region. Well, if you look at the diary, I don't ask you to do it now, I'd ask you to look in May. It's dated. The 12th of May is mentioned. The 14th May is mentioned. The 21st of May is mentioned. The 29th of May is mentioned. Interestingly, absolutely no mention of Fatmir Limaj coming to Lapusnik and saying I'm the boss. So once again just looking at that document alone it's rather like looking at (redacted) as an indicator of where the truth lies in this case, that a diary is a particularly salutary experience in terms of what he did and didn't do. And it's in that diary on page 17 although he was a little unwilling to admit it when I put it to him without showing him the passage he admits to beating the living daylights out of two prisoners in a bunker. Is this the kind of person you think may be telling you the truth? Although we say fairly little is said about Fatmir Limaj, but the little that is said in evidence about his command position is just not satisfactory. I'm looking at the clock. Is this convenient or would you like me to go a little longer?
