utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was dealing with the category of -- I've given the term victim-survivors, having dealt with L-64. There are in fact another six of these. I'm going to deal with them in some cases as a group, but there are distinctions. The first of this further six in the group, L-23, Ivan Bakrac and his father. This provides -- we put it first in the final brief and I put it first now certainly in relation to the rest of this group, because remarkably yesterday, the Prosecution still adhere to this extraordinary alleged identification. I want to go a little more slowly with this one because it's a demonstration of how you may in fact trim evidence when you are convinced that your evidence is going in the direction you want it to go in, in other words, you see what you want to see. So anxious are they that they have really missed, the Prosecution, the central point here, and I'll come to it in a moment. What happened is that when he arrived here at court, this is touching once again on this we say procedure which has no due-process protection, it's the proofing procedure, for the first time he explained that he had seen the person who he identified as the commander of the camp, which of course may not be the commander of any other area but that's how he was describing it, on the Internet. Now, the question that has to be posed, but of course we don't know whether it was during the proofing session because it wasn't fully and properly recorded. The first question you would want to ask as a Tribunal is the question, well, if you have identified Fatmir Limaj on an Internet photograph -- I leave aside when that happened because as the Prosecution have conceded there is a confusion as to when it is claimed it must have been seen, either in 1998 at the time or as he, Ivan himself says, 1999. So there is a real difference as to when that happened because he's linking it to 1999 because that's when they obtained a computer, so it's unlikely to have been before. However, I'm not going to spend time on when he claims he originally saw it. If he did see it either in 1998 or 1999, your question would be, well, why has it taken you until 2005 to mention it? Now, there is no answer to this. There is no explanation because it's worse than that. It's worse than not mentioning it till he gets here and having no real explanation as to why he didn't mention it till he got here. He was seen by the investigating authorities on the 10th and 11th of January, 2003, and he knew then that that's what they were investigating. So the most obvious thing if he is identifying, as far as he's concerned, the most important person in relation to the camp as he describes it, why doesn't he tell them? Oh, it's all right. I can tell you who it is. I've seen it on the Internet. So has my dad, as it happens. Something like that. It's the obvious thing to do. His answer to you about that, and he was asked by the Prosecution as to why he hadn't told the investigators that in 2003, was that he didn't have explanation. He didn't think it was important. Well, it's not adding up, as you may begin to realise. What we say has happened here, and this is the theme that attaches to many of these in this group, that is the six victim-survivors that the Prosecution use one way or another in relation to Fatmir Limaj, is that Fatmir Limaj, as you know from the evidence, clear, incontrovertible evidence, was on television on many occasions. He was a public figure. He was known. I concede not so much in 1998 and 1999 as 2000, 2001, 2002, and the further it gets from the war the more he is in the public eye. And what may have happened here is that there has been a discussion about the name, but more particularly what I'm going to suggest in his particular case has happened, he's identified a uniform, not a person. The reason we say this is that the Prosecution have forgotten what he told them, the man who he says was the commander of the camp, his description. I'll give you the transcript reference for this. It's T1430. He was asked to describe to you the person who he describes as the commander: "Can you describe his hair for us?" "Yes. He had longer, slightly longer hair combed back with some grey in it." This is the key question at this reference T1430: "And did he have any facial hair?" You will remember the Prosecution made great play about how somebody may be confused if the person had a beard and then they saw them in a lineup with no beard. Well, that's not the point. The person he says he saw as the commander had no beard. "Did he have any facial hair?" "No. He was clean-shaven." In fact he'd already given a description not dissimilar. As I've already indicated he was seen in January 2003. So what has happened here is if he's right, he's already seen the Internet photograph. So when he's shown a photo spreadsheet which has got Fatmir Limaj on it with no beard, and apparently the person he saw in the camp had no beard, how does he get confused because of the person in the Internet with a beard? You will appreciate at once what the Prosecution are saying here has absolutely no foundation. In other words, this is not a witness who has, as it were, seen somebody with a beard and when he's confronted with photographs of the same person without a beard is therefore unable to identify, because this is compounded three times over. So the clean-shaven commander, and it's true in evidence he said who had a camouflage uniform, which of course is in the clip on the Internet, but he goes on here to say, "Just as everybody else had." The only distinction he said was that his was neater. Whoever this person was that he's describing. So he's provided with the photo spreadsheet with Fatmir Limaj's photograph on it and doesn't identify Fatmir Limaj, the clean-shaven one. He is shown it again - so that's twice - here, but more important than that, he's actually asked to look around this courtroom, and he still doesn't identify Fatmir Limaj, and the Prosecution want you again to cherry-pick your way through this and rely on the own one he has picked out which has the beard and is not clean-shaven in the Internet short procession that is there. So we say here that this is an important non-identification. In other words, he's not in -- it's not just that he's not in a position. He is not identifying Limaj as the person he describes as the commander of the camp. So that's one more of the six, we say. And this is why we say so thoroughly that the Prosecution, at the rock bottom, have no rock, but I won't continue with the rest of the phrase. Now, we move to the next series of witnesses who are L-4, L-6, and L-10, and perhaps I can include also L-7. So it's a group of four. And again to try and save time, may I just pick out the common features here which give rise to serious question marks over these witnesses. And one appreciates plainly that where one or an individual may have been through a traumatic event it may be very difficult to remember detail. But it's much, we say, more significant than failure to remember detail. The common theme in this little group, that's 4, 6, 10, and 7, and there are some common features, firstly, there are serious inconsistencies between this group here, some of them not all, and what they said in previous statements. In particular, the absence on -- in some of these cases of any mention of a commander or Limaj or Celiku when they're first approached. So in other words, it's one thing to overlook a detail about the nature of the compound where you are or the exact order of events. It's quite another to fail to mention the person who it is suggested was either in charge of the camp or in charge of the area of responsibility under which the camp came. That's one point that arises with these witnesses. In particular so it's known, the ones where there is and inconsistent prior statement in relation to this is L-4 and L-10. Both fall into that category. Therefore, I'm not suggesting, because I'm trying to be consistent about this, that the prior statements become the truth. I don't ask you to do what I'm suggesting shouldn't happen in the hostile witness cases. Therefore, all one's doing with the prior statement is saying that if in fact when they come to identify Fatmir Limaj he was the person concerned, you have to explain in some of these cases why this was never mentioned when they were first approached about these events. So it becomes a serious credibility issue in the way that we suggest it should be for hostile witnesses. So that's one area of concern. What L-4 attempted to do in this area was to blame the interpreter because he doesn't, in his first statement, even mention a commander at all. Well, that doesn't, again, add up that the interpreter somehow or another has overlooked the mention of the word "commander," let alone any name attached to it. There are a number of other inconsistencies to do with who took him or claimed to have taken him to see the commander, whoever that was. He's given different accounts of that, being sure of each one, that they're different, different named people. He gives different accounts of conversations that he says he had with the commander, and these are all specified in our final briefs, so I'm not going to take up time to go through all the inconsistencies. So it's not just the inconsistency in terms of not mentioning a commander or the name of a commander before. There are others that should be added to this and accumulatively what he is saying in terms of Fatmir Limaj we say is not reliable. But that's just one aspect of this. The other aspect is already touched on by the Prosecution is in our final brief and that is the process of identification, because in three of these cases, that is 6 -- L-6, L-10, L-7, there were no identifications before they came here of Fatmir Limaj, and what happened when they came here is a dock identification. This can be dealt with very simply. Most jurisdictions are very reluctant to admit dock identifications as bearing any weight at all, one because it's obvious. Somebody's sitting in the dock and is alleged to be one of the perpetrators, although their three here. But it's fairly limited choice. And certainly those who sit in front are not going to be confused for the reason we're not in the dock in that sense. So therefore limited choice, dock identification is seen to be in a sense predisposing the witness. That's a very natural -- but it's compounded here, because once again all of these witnesses, 6, 10, and 7, all admit that they've seen, certainly by the time they get here, they've seen Fatmir Limaj many times, many times on television, national newspapers and so on. He is a well-recognised and recognisable figure who plainly occupies, hesitate to put it, centre stage but he's pretty close to the centre of the stage in Kosovo, so that he is a name to conjure with, he is a face to conjure with, and therefore the risk you have here is that people are identifying somebody who they've seen before, somebody in authority undoubtedly, and somebody who they think that since they've ended up here probably that's the person who they claim was the commander at the time or the person who they saw who was said to be the commander at the time. So in each of these cases, therefore, one needs to look very carefully to see whether they've mentioned a commander or the name of commander when they were first seen, and secondly, how they have come to identify and as you will see the identifications themselves are seriously dubious given the context in which they happen. There is, however, in this group of survivor witnesses somebody who merits a little more attention, and that is L-96. Now, I take a little more time on this particular figure because you may recall when he was opened, if I may put it that way, or when the Prosecution opened their case, although not now, this particular witness was suggested to be a central figure in this case. In fact, it was put, he's the reason we're all here. Well, if that's right that he's the reason we're all here, it's very interesting how he impinges or he doesn't impinge on Fatmir Limaj. I can dispose of the camp itself straightaway. He provided you with no evidence of Fatmir Limaj visiting the camp, being at the camp or doing anything at the camp at all. So if he's a central figure, he doesn't place Fatmir Limaj centrally. In fact, what it comes down to is a sighting, as you've heard many times now, on the mountain at the end, and it's the Berisha counts, if I can put it that way. Now, there's a bold attempt to try and shore up this witness, but of course what's been glossed over is a serious deficiency in what happened when he came here, and we say once again this demonstrates: Every single time you start to look at the wall of evidence, the bricks are falling away, and this is another one that falls away. Now, he gave you, and if I can just go back to the cross-examination on this. And I'm going to start at the end as it were. What he claims to you is that when he ran away, escaped from the mountains, the Berisha mountains, that he -- and this will bear upon whether in fact, of course, we say he ever saw Fatmir Limaj there or Fatmir Limaj had anything to do with whatever it was that happened in the mountains, he claims -- and the Prosecution don't really deal with this because they can't. You will recall he claims that what he did, and I asked him to trace it on these plans or maps, I don't ask you to look at them again, I hold them up, what he says he essentially did was he went across country. It's 40 kilometres, roughly speaking, back down to Ferizaj and so on down in the bottom right-hand corner. In that direction. And of course as he also admitted that if he's going to go like that as it were 40 kilometres, difficult terrain, who is controlling this terrain? The very people who he claims have just avoided executing him. So he's going through alien terrain on all fronts. We say this is, and to be blunt, a lie. He didn't do that at all. Now, if you find that he has lied, it matters not for what reason in one sense because it is a serious lie, but of course there are reasons why he may have lied, but once he's found to have lied thoroughly about what he did, you have to ask the same questions as you ask in hostile witness cases and in the Luan case, and in the, if I may put it shortly, the torturer case and so on and so on: Why has he lied and what was the lie? The lie is that of course he did something much more logical, and much more practical and much more immediate. On the 25th of July what he did looking at this same plan, it happens to be map 6, P1 map 6. Now what he did, he travelled a much shorter distance from the mountain as depicted in this plan to a Serb base on the Peja road at Komorane. Now, when I put that to him, of course he denied that because he was saying he'd gone across country. And of course this is getting into very tricky territory for him, was you may find that this particular witness in fact was not wanting it known that he had very close connection with some Serbs or his family did. And you recall that there were questions asked on that front, and to protect identity I'm not going to go through that area. But merely we say there's a very good reason why he didn't want to tell the truth here. He didn't want it known that in fact that what he had done was to give himself up to the Serbs. And he gave himself up to the Serbs, we say, because he knew that he was in fact going to get a better reception from them than anyone else. And interestingly, whose hands does he end up in? The very person that in fact the Prosecution now suggest, I think almost entirely shouldn't be relied on or at least only relied on in very limited circumstances. The interesting thing is that neither the person in whose hands he ended up, nor he, that is L-96, suggest that this particular Serb official practised any of the torture on him or even threatened him; quite the reverse. So someone doesn't have to investigate whether anything was done to provide this particular report. Now, the report I'm mentioning is in our final brief but not the detail of it. The report is dated, and you may have a record of it, the report itself, the 5th of August. In fact, it is suggested in the report that he came to the particular post in Ferizaj on the 1st of August. Now, you begin working backwards. You will see that there's a gap here because he's supposed to have escaped on the 25th of July. So we're dealing with a number of days, the 26th, the 27th, 928th, 29th, 30th, 31st of July until we get to the 1st of August. What is going on? And of course as you read the report you begin to see that what actually happened according to the report is that he went to that roadblock or at least that position, that Serb position, because that's what the report says he did, in Komorane, and the report indicates that at that checkpoint he told them what had happened. First account. Now, the importance of all of this is there is no mention of Fatmir Limaj or a commander who actually exercised authority over the fate of (redacted). It is inconceivable that if he knew -- because he spends time after the war apparently looking for the man responsible -- that he would not have been in a position straightaway. And even if he didn't do it when he gave himself up at the checkpoint. What then appears to have happened, and this explains the days that elapse between the 25th, not travelling across country the 40 kilometres and so on and so on and moving about without his papers which was his explanation, is that he then is seen by officials of the state security service. This is before he ever gets to Ferizaj. This is in Pristina. Who conduct a detailed interview with him. Once again, as far as can be told there is no suggestion at any of these stages that he's mentioned Fatmir Limaj or a commander who had the power to decide on life and death for (redacted). So that's the second stage. It's only at the third stage that he is seen in Ferizaj by this particular individual you know only too well and another. He is then, as it were, debriefed for a third time, and what is interesting about the third version, as far as we're concerned, and again I'm not asking that it's used as a substitute for anything, I'm merely indicating that if he's going to say now or even later that Fatmir Limaj is the man he identifies on the mountain as being the person deciding the fate of (redacted) effectively, then how come he doesn't tell the authorities on any of these three occasions? It's actually even more complicated than that. It's not that he doesn't mention. He doesn't talk about the incident at all in this first report. In other words, that halfway up the mountain a commander comes along and issues orders, this is the implication, whereby people then suffer the fate that is suggested. There is no incident on the mountain at all of a commander coming along. It's just not there. Now, this is not the day after he's been through a horrifying experience when, all right, you might forget something like that, you just might. This is on the third occasion, and it's several days, possibly a week later, and there's not a hint of this incident let alone the commander, as I say. There is also another interesting difference. Quite important, although perhaps not bearing directly on Fatmir Limaj. What he's told the Serb authorities was that the group that left the camp was divided up at the camp, and the details of that, again, are quite different to what he's now saying. Therefore, when one begins to even examine this particular witness, you have to examine whether he's told you lies, we say he has, about his movements; how it is that he hasn't mentioned Fatmir Limaj or a commander or the incident that the Prosecution rely so heavily upon, because if in fact the core of this is without foundation, struggling to find some other means of corroboration is really not an exercise that is merited. But of course he was seen by the investigating authorities after that. In other words, non-Serb authorities, by the CCIU, on the 20th of August, in the year 2000. And once again, he doesn't mention Fatmir Limaj or a commander of that kind. And one would have expected that once if his relationship with the Serbs might not have been as close as we submit it must have been to hand himself in, surely he would have started to mention the person who he regards or must have regarded as the most responsible (redacted). He would have mentioned it at the first opportunity when seen by the CCIU. And in -- once again we have this pattern reemerging that I've already mentioned in relation to L-4 and L-10, and that is an absence of early mention or early identification, and that the name Celiku or the identification of Celiku or Fatmir Limaj only comes out very slowly, and it comes out over a period of time. In this case, that is L-96, in 2002, and there is no doubt once again by that date that the name of Fatmir Limaj and his appearance is particularly well known and there is no dispute that he would have known that. And, one has to say - and I don't take time; some of these other details are in our final brief - that he has misidentified other people as persons concerned, no doubt from information that he may have got from other people. I'm not going to mention their names in open court but it's in our final brief. So he's liable to misidentify. He's liable not to identify people who he saw on his account far more often than the person on the mountain. And finally, of course, as we say, he didn't originally identify the incident on the mountain let alone the person. So we say fundamentally flawed, L-96. Central figure they may have wanted him to be, but you will have noticed by the end of case, certainly so far as Fatmir Limaj is concerned, he certainly does not provide that central core or basis. That brings me and if I may start, although I won't finish tonight but I will certainly finish in very short space of time tomorrow. It brings me to a -- a third -- a third and final area which is of some considerable importance and the reason why I will take a little more time on this. This is the section that we've already indicated has remained intact throughout the whole of the case, namely the nature of the person, Fatmir Limaj himself, and his personality, his credentials and so forth. And as I mentioned earlier today, we regard it as a key to the case and we ask you to consider it when you have then examined the flawed evidence I've just been through. I've left aside all the witnesses who support our case as opposed to the witnesses relied on by the Crown. We've mentioned them in our final brief. And of course one would need to dismiss those as well if one is going to cherry-pick through the ones I have mentioned. But one finally comes down to Fatmir Limaj himself, and as you mentioned he gave evidence over a long period of time. He spoke to you in opening. So you've had an excellent opportunity to get the measure of the man, if I may say so. The first important point about the measure of the man is that if we're right about his personality and character, then there has been a remarkable metamorphosis from somebody who led a lawful, responsible life before 1998. Even in the face of Serb oppression it is not suggested that he committed any unlawful acts. In the end he had to leave for reasons that he explained. And in the course of that pre-1998 explanation to you almost in passing he mentioned something almost in passing that you may think has a bearing, and that is that he and another were or did participate in what was called a blood-feud reconciliation initiative that was taken. And one recognises vendettas that occurred in the pre-1998 Albanian context. So this wasn't somebody who as it were utilised the excuse of a blood feud to exacerbate the situation. Quite the reverse. So from somebody who has acted responsibly and has been a student in fact dealing with matters of law at Pristina University before 1998, the moment he sets foot - this is the implication in the Prosecution case - the moment he sets foot in Kosovo he then apparently has this change. Almost Jekyll and Hyde, turns from being somebody who it's not even been a hint of activity of this kind. Very difficult to submerge the character that then apparently comes into being just for three months, four months. April, May, June July. He then becomes - and there is no other word for it if the Prosecution are right - a monster. He is prepared to if not actually establish, oversee the establishment according to them, of this prison camp and a system of inhumane treatment leading in some case to death. But it's even more -- I hope it's not another misdemeanour and I've mentioned something I shouldn't. I don't think I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I try worry about it. What happens is a metamorphosis again because within a month of this period of two months - you have these descriptions from others including the mountain teacher, of what he was doing for the people of Kosovo, I suggest as a whole, the 80.000 displaced people inside the country who needed shelter. He didn't go around asking them whether they were Serbs. He didn't go around asking whether somebody was an informer or need to be taken prisoner or whatever. He was, and there is no question about this, assisting in very large measure the civilians who had no where else to go but the valleys in the area where he basically had been brought up; born, brought up, and his family lived. And again, incontrovertible that he was doing this. How is this really possible, practically speaking, from a psychological point of view, that somebody switches and changes almost like a chameleon from one character to another character? There are circumstances, but they're very rare. They're unique, and we say if this was the kind of person that would supervise a prison camp of the kind described by the Prosecution, then the signs would have been evident either before 1998 and his return or very soon after this particular period, in 1998, 1999, 2000, and so on. So that's the first question that one has to pose, and that's why the nature and personality is important. There is a second feature here. Just think again if one can, and put oneself in his shoes in this period. If you accept, and I've already indicated some of the material suggesting that during -- during the war he was espousing, clearly, principles of justice, fairness, equality for all groups and therefore it's not surprising after the war that there was this minority statement from the Kosovo Assembly transitional authority that the Prime Minister, the ex-Prime Minister told you about supporting this man, Fatmir Limaj. He is running an extraordinary risk both at the time, if this is what he's doing supervising a prison camp, and incredible risk for a future political career of any credibility. The idea that you could supervise a camp of this nature and nothing ever got out about it and nothing ever got out about his role in it would be extraordinary risk for him to take given his ambitions, given where he wanted to go, and as I have said in the Rambouillet conference in 1999 what he was already trying to do. To stand up on the hustings as he already did on a number of occasion us and you've heard about it you've seen the election literature, you've seen -- in one case there is a photo of him standing alongside Madeleine Albright. Now, this is a man have a very high profile. Is he going to put all that at risk, that potential at risk if in fact he knows full well that in his own backyard he's done exactly the reverse of what he's exhorting his constituency to do. And we say, thirdly, of course, this character evidence is particularly relevant, and I've threaded it through the previous sections, in assessing the weight of the credibility of his denials of complicity in any camp. And I think there came a stage in the case where I endeavoured to make clear what his position is. You may understand that a man of this calibre, this stature, is really saying, when he's saying to you as he did, and there's no doubt about it before these proceedings formally began in this very courtroom, there was no camp. And I think yourself asked at some stage of me about the position. The position of our case is that he played no part in any prison camp. He finds it incredible that there would have been such a camp in such a place. And that is understandable. And what he's really saying is, "I don't know anything about it. And if I had, I would have done something about it given the kind of person I am." And therefore, it may be said well perhaps he should confront certain realities. It may be said in that same breath that this is a man who is, as the Prosecution is saying, lying, not confronting the truth and so on. But if he's right, it follows that he's not going to be in a position to accept that this has happened because he himself has played no part in it. So the denial he's made has to be seen against the person that he is. So it's these three features of the evidence as it affects him in relation to personality that has to be seen in the context. But there is an aspect of all of this that I've left until last at this moment but tomorrow afternoon I'd like to just deal with some of the aspects of his personality which support these contentions, these three contentions. I end tonight by just going back a stage in the chronology, and that is the question of his arrest. There is here a remarkable, if you like, cameo of Fatmir Limaj if you need one, to assess almost like a litmus paper test of the true character of the person and his responsibility, quite unlike and I'm not going to name others who have evaded arrest, not wanted to be arrested. I'm not talking about in particular Kosovo but elsewhere. What happened here, and you will note unchallenged when he gave this evidence, he was not cross-examined about any of this, despite the fact that originally, this is again almost the cherry-picking, the objection to provisional release partly was some suggestion that he was going to disappear, that he didn't give himself up in the one hour that elapsed between him discovering whilst he was on a short break which everyone knew about from the Prime Minister down to the person at the border. They all knew, the UNMIK general, they knew that he'd gone. Nobody stopped him. They knew where he was to the extent that a journalist was able to ring him up on his mobile and let him know that he was wanted. He didn't go to ground. He made public statements. And the most important thing he did at this stage which we say is a reflection of his genuine commitment not just because it's UNMIK or just because there's an international organisation but because he is concerned as always for the welfare of Kosovo, that what he did not want was a situation which could easily have erupted, as the Prime Minister said, in which people take to the streets, there is instability, there is in the end a situation in which the very fragile peace that has been sustained since 1999 could have been shredded by actions that he took, and he knew that you may think. And that is why, as the Prime Minister indicated, that he made a plea to the public that he was going to volunteer himself and the Special Representative Mr. Steiner knew this. And we've said it before and I say it again: What was reprehensible in this case was that the Special Representative did not come when summoned here to explain exactly what was known and the arrangements that was being made at that time, because effectively what he wanted, because he -- the flights as you may recall were not regular enough, he wanted one opportunity to go back to his family and to say good-bye before he came to The Hague. A perfectly reasonable possibility, and that the Special Representative at one stage was suggesting that he'd go and get him in a special plane. Well, none of that happened. He was arrested, but we say he did not need to be. And I say at this stage as well so that it's clear overnight that this particular aspect of the matter has meant that he has been already denied, we say, a form of justice. He should have been, and we say would have been in the same position as another defendant, namely Mr. Haradinaj, awaiting trial; not in custody. Given his background and given his commitment and given what his attitude was to the knowledge that he was wanted and his respects for this Tribunal and the fact that he has, if cooperation is the right word, given evidence at here at some length and has constantly referred to the fact that he respects the reason and the objectives of this Tribunal, and of course this whole area as I've said was not suggested to him in cross-examination, that any of this was rubbish. Therefore, we say he's already waited in custody a very long time. And we say that's a highly prejudicial situation, and it goes back to the question of the even-handedness and also the approach to cases like this, because what then happens is even worse. He's in custody and then there are allegations, and I don't shy away from the allegations, allegations that were made originally that this very Tribunal in the end fortunately brought some justice to this situation, allegations that in some way or another he was responsible for intimidation and possibly that might be affecting the evidence. And it was said by Mr. Cayley this material was going to be led in evidence. "Will be led" were his words. Well, it hasn't been led, and yet it led to a regime of incommunicado with his family. It may have been the reason for blindfolds and so on, the matters that concerned us so much at the beginning, and we say gave an aura of predisposition by the Tribunal to his particular case. And it's fully understandable that that is something that he and others around him should feel about what had already happened. And we say that is not an example which should not be followed. And the request that I make to Your Honours, finally tonight, is this: That if there is to be between the ending of oral submissions this week and the delivery of your judgement in this case an appreciable and I'm not in a position to say what it would be, but an appreciable interval of time that consideration even at this late stage might be given to the possibility of provisional release for him at least for that short time so he can be with his family which is where he should have been up to now and in light of the fact there is frailty and illness particularly and illness amongst his parents. If there is to be an appreciable interval then we are proposing that we would certainly in writing ask that this be reconsidered even though it is an unusual situation - it's not unprecedented - an unusual situation, but it might just begin to repair the injustice that we say has been meted out to him in this case already and at least would afford him some time to as it were face whatever judgement it is you intend to apply to this case in either a month or two months or whatever the time scale is. I wonder at this juncture whether I might defer the remainder of what I have to say about his personality and the evidence that relates to that until tomorrow. It will take probably no longer than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Mansfield. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 31st day of August, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
